OUR Gia-lis.—Existence was never originally meant to -be that useless, blank, pale, slow-strafing thing it often , becomes to many. . . Fathers, you would wish to be "proud or your daughters, and not blush for them; then seek for them an interest and an occupation which shall raise them above the flirt. the maeceuvrer, the mischief- making tale-bearer. Keep your girls' minds narrow and fettered—they will be a plague and a care, sometimes a disgrace, to you; cultivate them, give them scope and -work—they will be your gayest companions in health, your tenderest nurses in sickness, your most faithful -prop in age. Cfi.7e a woman a good mental trainirg, give her the power of employing whatever talents are entrusted to Let, and no outward circumstances can -make her useless or unriappy.—Churchtnan's Magazine. A West of :•corland clergyman was going to the High- lands for his holidays, and b jug very fond of the Nabob Pickles." 14e took a bottle with him. The Nabob .Pickles" are extremely hot, and should be very sparingly used. Arrived at an hotel, he placed the bottle .on the-table, and took one or two of them. A Yankee was sitting opposite, end got his eye on the mckles. -"Stranger, pass the pickles, please. The clergyman said, "These are private property, but you are welcome to them." He passed the bottle across the table. The Yankee emptied half the b,4tle into his plate. and stirred them well up with hitaspoon. Betook a big spoonful,

but they were not long down when he drew, ,a long breath and said, "Oh, dodgest it! Look here, stranger, I guess you are a parson?" "Well, I am a clergyman, find I preach the getpel." -"Look you here," said the Yankee, "I have heard theta preach about fire and brimstone. but you are the only one I know who carries ra sample battle." THE PYRAMID AND THE Ommisit.—l have thought a good deal about Egypt, lately, with reference to our historical monuments. How did the great unknown masters who fixed the two leading forms of their monu- mental records arrive at those admirable and eternal types, the pyramid and the obelisk'? flow die they get heir model of the pyramid? Here is an hour-glass, not napprepriately filled with sand tram the great Egyptian desert. I turn it. and watch the sand as it accumulates in the lower half of the glass. Haw symmetrically, how beautifully, how inevitably the little particles pile up the cone, which is ever building and uribuilding always aiming at the stability which is found only at a certain fixed angle! The Egyptian children playing in the sand must have noticed this as they let the grains fall from their hands, and the sloping sides of the miniature pyramid must have been among the familiar sights to the little boys and girls for whom the sand fur- nished their earliest playthings. Nature taught her -children through the working °tithe laws of gravitation how to build so that her forces should act in harmony with art, to preserve the integrity of a structure meant to reach a far-off posterity. The pyramid is only the cone in which Nature arranges her heaped and sliding fragments; the cone with flattened surfaces, as it is pre- figured in certain well-known crystalline forms. The obelisk is from another of Nature's patterns; it is only a gigantic acicular crystal.—Oliver W. Holmes, in the Atlantic Monthly,

Miss "Edna Lyall" has been for several weeks incapacitated by serious illness from all literary work, and is still lying ill at her home, College- road, Eastbourne. She is too prostrate to reply to current attacks regarding her theological opinions.

Mr. Geo. Lane Pox, the Vice-Chancellor of the Primrose League, is esteemoi as a delightful and racy companion by his friends. He has been a real martyr for conscienee sake, having of his.own free will dispossessed himself of £IO,OOO per year by joining the Roman Catholic Church.

Miss Mary Anderson is expected to reach London next week, and her marriage with Mr. Navarro will be celebrated at Brompton Oratory during the month of May. Among the popular actress's bridesmaids will be one of the daughters of Lord and Lady Lytton, who are old friends of hers. " Our Mary" is in her thirty-second year, and has been on the stage for fourteen years, making her first appearance as Juliet at a Louisville theatre.

It is generally believed that Germany is the "Great Power" to which the secret plan for the defence of Cronstadt was treacherously sold by a Russian naval officer, and, if this be so, the fact forms a queer commentary upon the Emperor William's effusive professions of friendship for Russia. It is no secret, however, that the Czar has the greatest aversion for the Emperor person- ally, and the old family alliance between the Romanoff and the Hohenzollern is now entirely at an end.

Lady Fanny Majoribangs. wife of the popular Liberal Whip, at whose house Mr. Gladstone on Saturday met Lord Randolph Churchill and Mr. John Dillon, forms a happy link between the two political parties. Whilst her husband is a prop of the Liberal party, her brother—Lord Randolph Churchill—is, not exactly a prop of the Conserva- tive party, but still an important member of it. Lady Fanny Marjoribanks is a thorough-going Liberal, and'ae popular in society as her husband is in the House.

" T.D.S."—as Mr. T. D. Sullivan is affectionately known to all his colleagues—took formal farewell last week of the " Nation," with which he has been associated for upwards of thirty years. He announces that he has sold the paper to Mr. Lalor, who has been on the business staff for a consider- able period, and that the editorship will be in the hands of Mr. Robert Donovan. Mr. Sullivan vouches for Mr Donovan's entire fitness for the post. Mean- time T. D. S. promises to occasionally fill a corner in the ,columns of the time-honoured Journal.

"I own 20,000 hectares of forest," said Prince Bismarck to M. Jules Simon, "and I plant were trees than I cut down." Upon which a sarcastic Tory asked whether M. Jules Simon's thoughts re- verted to another statesman who has cut down more trees than he has planted, and remarks that herein lies a parable. Possibly; but if you mention the =atter of cutting down trees to Mr. Gladstone lie will tell you—it my be rather eagerly—that he never in his life cut down a tree which was not in need of cutting. Perhaps herein, too, lies a parable.

The most original speech at the election of the Society for Women's Suffrage was that of Mrs. Mas- singbird, of Gunby, who introduced herself as a curious illustntion of the justice of her fellow- countrymen. The owner of hundreds of acres, of houses in three counties, with a tolerable know- lee of the Queen's English, and ability to read and write, and, moreover, permitted to keep her own surname and use her own arms, Mrs. Massing- bird considers it a crying shame that she is not allowed what the poorest labourer on her estate can claim—the right to rote. With great humour and eloquence she urged her audience to join in the struggle.

Although Mr. Santley is coining money in the colonies and singing to enthusiastic audiences, he is not without his little legal troubles. A few months auo, he had his first manager arrested (Mr. E. Price, of the Australian entertainment Bureau) for frau- dently appropriating the proceeds of some of his concerts,,but the magistrates dismissed the case. Now Price is going for the eminent baritone to the tune of ..£5,000 damages for false imprisonment, malicious Kosecution, and breach of contract. Be- fore Mr. Santley was permitted to leave Melbourne for hie New Zealand tour, a Judge of the Supreme Court ordered him to deposit X 50,0 as bail fer his re- appearance in Australia to answer these charges.

New that everybody has something to tell of Prince Bismarck, people are reviving a story of him during the Franco-German war. One night, it is said, in the very heat and fury of the bloody struggle, he found an infant lying upon his bed with a note pinned to its swaddling clothes stating that the child's name was Vincent, and that its father had been killed at Sedan. The Prince referred the case to King William, whose reply was, "Keep him. In war time you must take whatever you can get, even if its only a child." Accordingly Vincent was sent to Berlin, and brought up at Prince Bismarck's expense. He is now one of the Prince's most devoted attendants, and lately followed him into his retirement at 'Friedrichsruhe.

' Referring to Lord It. Churchill's speech on his Licensing till, on Tuesday, the "Star" says:— To see a Tory leader going full tilt at the house of the publican was an astonishing and appetising a sight as the historic foray of the Druid King upon the sacred Tessels and symbols of the Druid altars. The Tories seemed to have a very different feeling, for while the Liberal benches were crowded, the Tory rank and file was conspicious by absence. How- ever, as the evening wore on, things changed, and Lord Randolph had a very full house. But the temper of the two sides was very different. The Liberals cheered withoutstint, while the Tories listened in ghastly silence—except when Lord Randolph pro- claimed himself a friend to the principle of compen- sation. The speech was very carefully prepared, and lasted for an hour and three-quarters. There were many extracts from Blue-books. Parliamentary speeches, and the like -and the work of quotation is not enlivening. But it was an admirably arranged speech.

A prisoner promoting one of his gaolers to a governorship sounds like a Gilbertian paradox, yet it has actually happened in Australia. The recent death Of Mr. John Lovett, Governor of Darlinghurst Gaol, Sydney, recalls the fact. Some years ago a well-known public man of New South Wales, Mr. G. R. Dibbs (now leader of the Opposition in that colony) refused to pay what he believed to be an unjust aud extortionate bill of costs, and was com- mitted to Darlingburst Gaol for contempt of court. There he remained for twelve months, working in the carpenter's shop. After his release he re-entered public life, became Prime Minister, and, as luck would have it, he was called upon to appoint a new Governor at Darlinghurst Gaol, owing to the retire- ment of Sir John Cecil Read. Be remembered the good qualities of the warder who had charge of him as a prisoner, and promptly promoted Mr. Lovett to the vacant post. Has any Irish warder similarly favourably impressed John Dillon or William O'Brien

The late Mr. Joe Ronayne, member for the City of Cork, as one of the wittiest and most good- humoured of men, but though Mr. O'Connor Power sat with him in the House of Commons for years, he never once heard him do justice to his powers. He was out of harmony with the tone of the House, had no contact with it at all, and Mr. Power cites the authority of Mr. Parnell himself for the fact that " Joe Ronayne " was the first to suggest to him the policy of Parliamentary obstruction. Mean- while, in Irish gatherings outside Parliament, and in the society of his friends, Joe's genial and pungent wit was, we are told, in full force. He died from the effects of the amputation of a leg. When the doctors had decided to cut it off, a friend said to him, "Joe, I am particularly sorry your leg has to be cut off." " Why are you particularly sorry r inquired the sufferer. " Because," said his friend, "you will never be able to stand forthe city again." To which Joe, turning in the bed on which he ex- pired a day or two later, quietly replied, " Sure if I can't stand for the city I can stump the country."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 3, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 3, 1890
DEATH OF EDWIN WAUGH.

Mr. Edwin Waugh, widely known as "The Lancashire l'oet," died on Wednesday night, about eight o'clock, at his residence in New Brighton. Mr. W augh had suffered for a considerable time from cancer of the tongue, and during the past few weeks it was known to his near friends that his end was approaching. Numerous daily inquiries have been lately made as to his condition, by friends and admirers in various parts of the country, and much sympathy was extended to him in his prolonged ill- ness. He became a permanent resident of New Brighton some years ago, in the hope that his health would be benefited by the change. Mr. Edwin Waugh's literary and poetic genius has been an inspiration to Lancashire people for very many years, and the popularity of his Lanca- shire sketches and other writings has made his name a household word throughout the greater part of the county. He had attained the ripe age of seventy-three, with an intellect so unimpaired and a constitution so robust that, but for the malady which attacked him in his later years, and for which he underwent two operations, he might have been expected to continue to delight his vast array of admirers for some time to come.

Mr. Waugh was born and reared near Rochdale, where a considerable portion of his early prime was spent, and where much of that process of self- education which has had such delightful results for Lancashire people was carried on. For two or three years prior to his removal to New Brighton he lived at Kelsall, near Manchester, a place con- venient to the busy cottonopolis, where his charming poems and sketches, produced with un- failing regularity, continued to the last to be in universal request, and whence they were dissemi- nated to an extent which told its own tale of the high pinnacle of fame on which popular opinion had placed him. In the salu, rious air of New Brighton, which combined for him the great ad- vantage of health with ready accessibility to Liver- pool and Manchester, he enjoyed life amazingly, though in a very quiet and unostentatious fashion. One of his favourite modes of meditation and study was to take a quiet walk by the seashore, from which, while nnding that rapture which Byron speaks of, he may be said to have picked up ideas for the enrichment of his literary productions very much as other people pick up shells and pebbles. The following sketch of the deceased appears in " Men of the Time ":—Edwin Waugh was born January 29th. 1817, at Rochdale; is descended from a Border family long settled upon their own land, near Haltwhistle. He was educated at Daven- port's Commercial Academy, at Rochdale; was apprenticed to a bookseller and printer; and after his apprenticeship worked as a printer and book- seller-for nearly ten years. He was then appointed secretary to the Lancashire Public School Associa- tion, for the promotion of a national plan of secular educatlon. He was connected with this association for nearly five years; since then he has devoted himself entirely to literature. Mr. Waugh received a pension of £9O from the Civil List in 1882. He is the author of " Lancashire Sketches," " Poems and Lancashire Songs ;" "Tufts of Heather," a series of tales ; "Factory Folk during the Cotton Famine ; " "Rambles in the Lake Country; " "Snowed up and other Tales; " "Rambles and Reveries ; " " Sancho's Wallet," a series of Northern anecdotes ; " The Chimney Corner," a series of coun- try tales ; " Roads out of Manchester; " " An Old Math; Memories ;" and " The Limping Pilgrim." In politics, Mr. Waugh wa.s an ardent Liberal, though he did not seem to have carried his enthusi- asm to the point of appearing on public platforms. He was, however, a Radical of the old Manchester school, and a warm friend of his distinguished 'townsman John Bright, and was proud of a letter written him by that illustrious statesman from Llandudno not long ago. He also enjoyed the friendship of Mr. Jacob Bright, and of many others eminent in literature, politics, and music. He was for some time an active member of the Manchester Literary Club, and some years ago filled with acceptance the honoured position of its president. Mr. Waugh was last in public at the Parnell ban- quet at the Reform Club, on which occasion he presented to the illustrious Irish leader a copy of his poems, including the very apt one for the gath- ering, " Old Ireland shall blossom again." Mr. Waugh and the late Mr. McMinnies, of War- rington, had been long and intimately acquainted, and, as we mentioned at the time of Mr. McMinnies death, one of Mr. Waugh's volumes on the Lanca- shire Cotton Famine was dedicated to his old friend. The last time they saw each other, and had " a crack" together, was in September of last year, when Mr. Waugh paid his last visit to Warrington. Mr. H. Bona, of this journal, has set several of Mr. Waugh's songs to music, and the immediate occa- sion ot the poet's visit was to go over with Mr. Bond his setting of "Keen blows the north wind," and "Oh, the summer is sweet." He expressed himself as pleased with the music, and said he would immediately arrange for its publication. Mrs. Waugh had meantime gone to see Mr. Speak- man, of the Saracen's Head, to whom she is related. Mr. Waugh, as we have stated, called upon Mr. McMinnies, and spent some time with him before returmng,with Mrs. Waugh, to New Brighton. That be had more than an ordinary regard for Mr. Mc Minnies may be inferred from the fact that in con- versation with the Editor of this journal, at New Brighton, last summer, he said, on Mr. McMinnies name being mentioned—" He is a fine man, is Mr. • McMinnies; one of the finest in Lancashire. Tell him I often think of him, and that I always think of him with pleasure." . Among the many poetical productions written, by him in the local dialect none perhaps reached the hearts of the Lancashire people so readily as that entitled •".Come whoam to thi childer' an me." Such was its extreme popularity for years after it was published that in all probability it would have made a name for him even if it had been the first meritorious work which be had produced. Upwards of a quarter of a century has passed since it first saw the light, and yet its popularity seems more extensive than ever, since the rising generation of the cotton manufacturing districts have it im- pressed upon them as a production that they ought to learn by heart. It will, therefore, bear reprint- ing in the present circumstances.

COME WHOAM TO THI MILDER AN' ME. Aw've just mended th' fire wi' a cob; Owd Swaddle has brought thi new shoon ; There's some nice bacon collops o' th' hob, An' a quart o' ale posset th' oon ; Aw've brought thi topcoat doesto know, For th' rain's cornin! deawn very dree ; And th' harthstone's as white as new snow : Come whoam to thi childer an' me. When aw put little Sally to bed Hoo cried 'cose her feyther weren't theer ; So aw kissed th' little thing, an' aw said Thae'd bring her a ribbin fro' th' fair; An' aw gave her her doll an' some rags, An' a nice little white cotton bo', An' aw kissed her again; but hoo said 'At hoo wanted to kiss thee an' o'. An' Dick, too, aw'd sich wark wi' him Afoar aw could get him upstairs ; Thae towd him thae'd bring him a drum, He said, when he're sayin' his prayers ; Then he looked i' my face, an' he said— " Has th' boggarts taen houd o' my dad ?" An' he cried till his een were quite red ; Ho likes thee some wee!, does yon lad! At th' lung length aw geet 'em laid still, And aw hearken't folks' feet that went by, So aw iron't o' my clooas met well, An' aw hanged 'em o'th maiden to dry. When aw'd mended thi stockins and shirts, Aw sit deawn to knit i' my cheer An' aw rayley did feel raythur hurt— Mon, aw'm lonely when theaw artn't theer. "Aw've a drum an' a trumpet for Dick, Aw've a yard o' blue ribbin for Sal, Aw've a book full o' babs an' a stick, An' some bacco and pipes for mysel'. Aw've brought thee some coffee an' tay,— Iv thae'll feel i' my pocket thae'll see— An' aw've brought tho a new cap to-day, But aw al'ays bring summat for thee. "God bless tho', my lass; aw'll go whoam, An aw'll kiss thee an' th' childer o' round; Ths.e knows that wherever aw roam, Aw'm fain to get back to th' owd ground; Aw can do wi' a crack o'er a glass, Aw can do wi' a bit of a spree; But aw've no gradely comfort, my lass, Except wi' yon childer an' thee.'

Iv ther's one thing o' th' world as wimmen like —ay, an' men, too, but moor 'specially wimmen— it's mekkin' bergains ; they'll gooa ceawerin',o' day at a sale-room to save a penny, when they owt to be at hooam dernin th' eh ilder's stockins,or stitchin' buttons on their husband's shorts. Like as it's born fooak to want to ged a sixpenny artickle for' a penny : they ne'er think, cr keer, whooa loyses th' fippence on id, an' as often as nod—a lot oftener— they ged suckt in. Chaps 'll speculate i' things they're nod pertielerly wantin' when they think o' mekkin' a snap; 'appen it's an owd sailor (?) as hes some smuggled silk hankitchers, wo'tli five shillin' apiece, to sell at ninepence, or some smuggled 'bacca at a shill in' for hafe-a peawnd— deawn gooas th' brass, an' when th' chap shows his wife at th' hankitchers boo tells him wheer boo con buy hofe-a-dozen for wod he's paid for one ; an' it's just th' same wi' his chep ' 'bacca —it's ayther cabbige, lettice, or tay /eeaves. As for th' wimmen they'll buy owt for th' sake o' mekkin' a bergain ; they co'id savin' a bit o' sum- mat. But this isn'd th' wo'st soort o' their 'economical werk, for yo may send 'em to a auction- room wi' nobbut hofe-a-creawn i' their pockets, an' abeawt four or five heawrs at after they'll come lorryin' hooam wi' th' followin' : A clock, A pair o' ballis, A umbrella, A pair o' boots, A sause-pon, an' no less nor thrippence change! Fost ov o' yo' find as th' clock lies imitated thad as yo' read abeawt th' song—it's stopt short ne'er to gooa ageean ; yo' give a chap sixpence for boilin' id, an' as thad does no good yo' tek id to a jeyveller, an' he charges goodness nobbut knows heaw"mich. Th' ballis hes chronic congestion o' th' lungs, but yo'r wife 'll set to werk on id wi' a stockin' needle an' some wustid ; th' cobbler hes to petch id up at last, an' he cherges as mich as iv he'd soiled a pair o' shoon. Then yo' find as th' umbrella hes some com- peawnd fractures o' th' ribs, wants a fresh stick, and recoverin' ; as th' pair o' boots is ayther booath lefts or reights—an' yo con fancy wod id wod cost to advertise i' th' pappers for th' mon as hes t'other two lefts or reights. An' th' wost thing ov o' is to find as th' saucepan hes a little hoyle Pth' bottom on't, for yo ve never 4one bevin' th' plumber i'th heawse to so'der thad pun; a plumber con spend hofe a day onytime petchin' up a little hoyle wi' rozin an' lead.- Iv yo're one o' them chaps as books o' these things deawn, yo'll find as this hofe-creawn's watt hes cost nearer two peawnd—in fact,thad sum wod ha' bought 'em new fro a good shop, an' fro' a hire system place they wodn'd ha' cost mich moor nor four or five peawnd. div.p: THE BIRMINGHAM TRAGEDY.

James Jones, alias "Big Jonah," who is charged with killing a man named Grice in Summer-lane, Birmingham, on Saturday night, was captured at Sheffield on Monday morning. He admitted he was the person wanted for the crime, but said the fatal blow was only struck after Once had hit him. When brought before the Sheffield Stipendiary the accused seemed very unconcerned. He was ordered to be sent to Birmingham.

div.head: STEP-FATHER'S CLAIM.
div.p: A STEP-FATHER'S CLAIM.

In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. Justice Day and a special jury, the case of Lock v. Julius Hohmann, a claim by a step-father, wh is a publican at Dalston, for damages for the seduction of his step-daughter, came on for hearing. It was alleged that defendant, a wine merchant's manager, went away with a girl named Ada Victoria Rawlinson to Brighton, saying they were to be married, but the marriage never took place. A verdict for the plaintiff was returned, damages 2300.

.... " Does he?" replied Mark, dreamily. "Ruth, my child," he continued, "you have done wrong—very wrong—in parting with this money. Martin should have had no debt of honour to pay that would c,llfot the little dowry of an orphan girl." "But he would have been dishonoured if he had not paid, Mark." "He was more dishonoured in robbing you, my child," said Mark, sternly. "Oh, no, no, no! Don't speak like that, Mark," sh( cried, excitedly. "it is only a loan. He assured me that he should soon have money again, when it would be replaced. He said that he would not have taker that last hundred if he had not I,efin sure."

"And you believed him, Ruth?" "Oh, yes, Mark," she cried, quickly. "I am our: Martin will repay me. You do not know his charactei so well as I." "Perhaps not," he said sadly, for these words stung him bitte ly. "Are you not a little too hard upon poor Martin?' " No, my child, I fear that I am not. Ruth, m 3 dear, you must know the truth sooner or later, so I tel you now, although I know I ant giving yi,u great pain Martin has somehow been led into courses that mean his ruin."
"Oh Mark l" she cried, piteously. " It is too true, Ruth," he qaid, firmly, "and it resh with you to help me to lead him back to a stead, course."
"Oh yew," elle cried ; "I will try so very hare Mark. I do try indeed." "You love Martin," he raid, after a paure...
"Oh, :c es, indeed I do, Mari," she said, looking al it bim pleadingly. "Poor fellow! he is BO dferentle you biz lam sure he means well." Mark closed his eyes for s morneni.
"Yes," he said, with a sigh; ''but tsll me, Ruth, win this the drst time tpat Martin had asked you for Inoue) ?'
Ruth looked at him beseechingly, but remained

You have over a hundred pounds in the bank— my mother' gilt." She i6ook be head, the tears standing in her eyes. INila:k began to pace up and down the room. "Martin has had ,that, then ?" he said, at last. "Ye, Mark," she faltered. "Not all ?" he said.
"Yes; all Mars," she replied, in a low voice; "but don't be angry, I don't want it. Poor Martin is welcome to it all and more if it was mine." " When was this?"
" Six months ago, Mark." "Oh, Ruth, Ruth. Ruth, my child," be cried, as be strode up and down the room; "this is indeed dreadful.'

" Oh, no, no, she cried, going up to him, and clinging to his arm. "Do not speak or think of it like that. Dear Mark, you should have had all I possetsed in a moment if you had wanted it. Martin was in such trouble that! was only too glad to be able to help him." " My dear child," he said, angrily, "I hare neg. tented my tru,t in letting him rob you like this." "Rob? Oh, ark!""d "it is nothing else," he cried, angrily. "Where has the money gone but to some of his low, gambling associates?"

"Oh, Mark, you are unjust," she faltered. " No," he said, bitterly, "I am weak. I ought to have foreseen that he would endeavour to win from you your little store. Ruth, Ruth, what have I done that you did not confide in me?"
"What could I do?" she said, inirsting into tears. "He told me of his distress, and begged ot me to help him." _

"You should have come and consulted me, my child," he said, tenderly, laying his hand upon her glossy hair, and gazing dcwn at her with a tevder yearning in his eyes that was piteous in the extreme; for the love she showed for his brother stirred him to his deepest depths, all the time that he was fighting against himself, and manfully striving for her happi- ness "Ruth, my dear," he said, sadly. "have I acted of late so as to make you mistrust me?" "Oh no, no, Mark," she cried. "I felt that I ought to tell you, and said so, but poor Martin begged so bard that I would say nothing. He told me that, you would be angry—that you could not undersfand his diffi- culties, and that you would blame him for what he had done."

" Naturally," said Ram. "I did want to take you into my confidence, but he said he would sooner suffer all that might come upon him than you should know." " And so you gave way, Ruth," said Mark, sadly. "I do not blame you, my child; I was to blame. I ought to have had more foresight. There, there, little one, go and bathe those eyes and dry those tears. This must be a little secret between us. Aunt must not be told."

She looked up at him 11l a frightened, piteous manner—a look that be did not then understand, for months of weariness and trouble had to pass More the scales fell from his eyes--the eyes with which he stood gazing after her sorrowfully, as she stood for a moment as if about to tell him something, and then left the room.
CHAPTER XVII. A TOUCH IN THE DARE.

IT was past twelve, approaching one o'clock, and Mark Woolf ord sat alone in the little dining-room trying to think out his brother's future. Matters seemed to be getting to a climax; for Martin must be mixed UD in gambling transactions of some kind to a far worse ex- tent than he had realised. Ile knew, of course, of a grea;.. deal of money thrown away. He had wasted hundreds in helping Martin himself, but this plundering of poor little Ruth came upon him like a revelation, and, in spite of his endeavour to think well of the young man, and to treat these lapses as escapades of a boyish nature, the truth would force itself hoine that Martin was as unprinoi pled as could be. It was a hard task, and the eudiculties at the °Moe seemed to be increasing. Even the knowledge that he had made an enemy of the weak drunkard, the porter, was, at such a time, full of trouble, for be knew that little insects would sometimes sting most painfully. "They all talk about the lenience shown to Martin," he said, bitterly. Just then, as his mind was running in the direction of whether it would not be betkr after all to try and get Martin abroad, he rose and crossed the room to an old desk—his late father's, and in which his mother bad been in the habit of keeping her letters and memo- randa.

He opened it with a feeling of reverence, and, after a little hesitation, as if it were almost sacrilege, he took out a little book of private memoranda containing pencil entries made by the dead. Yes, there they were, all in the familiar hand: every pound that she had expended scrupulously accounted for; and amongst the entries repeated until he felt heartsick at seeing their frequency, these were the records of the supplies given to Martin. There was the mother's weak love for her boy told ha every page, till Mark closed the book with a weary sigh, looked it up, and returned to his seat with the knowledge that his brother's follies had been far worse than he bad ever dreamed.

"1 must judge him sternly," he said; "or I shall be doing wrong." For that very day he had sat by Mr. Klopstocrs bedside, begging leniency for his brother, and now, in the silence of the night, he was alone with his con- science, asking, himself for the hundredth time whether a man who gambled was one fit to be in the office? And next, was one who did not scruple to prevail upon an innocent young girl to part with her little dowry„ a fit person to hold a situation of trust? No! He stirted, for the word his own lips had uttered seemed to have come from another source. He wee not at heart one who would have judged leniently of another's failings, for he was too stern a believer in duty; and as he sat there with the recol- lection of Benison Hall's escapade coming before him, as if to corn pare itself with the behaviour of his brother, he recalled how he had dealt very seriously with a piece of negligence on the porter's part. "What am I to do about him now?" he asked. He determined upon a severe reprimand, and, indeed, report the case to Mr. Klopstock. "lam going wrong, too," he said, thoughtfully, for be knew that he was disarmed from a just treatment in the porter's offence by his partial dealings with his brother.

"I'll sit up for him to-night, and have a quiet talk," he said; and taking out his watch, he saw that it was dose upon one. It was dreary work waiting, for his thoughts were very sad. He dreaded the interview, but still be felt that it must take place, for after the revelations made by Ruth, he knew that he would be still more wanting in his duty if be refrained from speaking. "Martin's present course means social ruin, and now or never his course must be stayed." The lamp was begiuning to burn dimly, and he set to work and trimmed it. Then he set the door slightly open, so that he might be sure to hear anybody who came in. Then, placing the shade over the lamp, he took up a favourite work and sat down to read. It was a vain effort: his eyes passed over the lines, but not a word did he comprehend; and, at last, he impatiently threw the book aside, to sit wondering whether his brether would return. As he sat there he felt a strange kind of nervoue

agitation seize upon him, and though at another time he would have been ready to laugh at such ideas, he now found himself recalling and pondering aver Miss Klop-tock's words, and their prophetic import. "Something is going to happen!" she had said. Was it possible that this was the case, and that these apparently trivial puerile warnings came in advance? It might be possible, but he smiled as he thought it,, and began to recall what Miss Kloostcck had said. • Strange how he kept thinking of the old man then. He hoped he was not worse. He had said that they would both repent not taking stronger measures about Martin. Was anything going to happen to him or , through him? Had anything happened to him that he did not return ? " What an old woman I am becoming!" he said. getting up to pace the room. "Mv nerves inus, be out of order. lam as weak as a child." It was no new thing though, or of old, when, he had come home extra worried and troubied by cln:.o application to business, a nervous :tate of excitemeat-, attacked him, and very often this took the form 01 s dre-d lest anything should have happened at the , office. Now it would be fire, now burglary; always some- thing that he laughed at himself for thinking when the next day came, though at the time the dread was • • . very real. He knew that with the precaution taken by the old manager, there ought to be no danger. especially now that Mr. Mithllecombe's vault was , perfect, and everything of importance was stored there , night by night; but still the thoughts would come. In a curious vague fashion, the fit came upon him this night with redoubled violence; and so great was the nervous excitement at last, as he eat watching there. that he felt as if he could hardly bear it. He paced the room with more rapid strides; then

piu he listened to a passing cab; then a footstep struck his ear, but neither cab nor stop stayed at the door, and feeling that a good sharp walk in the cool air might refresh him, and relieve the peculiar sensation from which he was suffering, he walked softly into the hall. Here he listened, but all was very still, as he put on his overcoat and hat, feeling for his latch-key, and hoping that, upon his return, he should find Martin at home. It was not the first time by many that he had done this, and a sharp walk was certainly the best medicine for his complaint. Going back into the little dining-room he turned out his reading lamp, and then returning gently to the passage so as not to disturb those above, he was on his way to the front door, when he fancied that he heard a faint rustling noise. He stood listening, and holding his breath. Martin must have slipped in quietly as he was turning out his lamp, but it was strange he thought that he had not heard the click of the door. There it was again—a faint rustling noise. How cautious he was, for he felt that it must he Martin, everyone else had been in bed for the past two hours. It was something novel for the young man to be so careful as to awakening those in the house when he came home.

"Rustle, rustle, rustle, but going to, not coming from, the front door. It was intensely dark, and Mark felt puzzled, as hi wished for a match to use. Was he rni,taken. and this was not Martin? Suppose instead o;' the of3l-' being in danger, the clanger was here in their owa place. At any rate, i it is, thought Mark-, I will know the worst; and listening attentively a= the rustlinit noise continued, be suddenly stretched forth his ivied in the darkness to feel it come in contact with another. Which he immediately gra:Ted. (lo overiz,:lced.)

rfaalt tow and then Miss Klopstock used, now tbal ehe was settled down in Brunswick-rquare, to devote an evening to what che called "totting up" the cc. uounts, the said accounts being the weekly bills of the 4utcher, baker, greengrocer and others ; and the clifil• willies the poor lady got into were terrible. Miss Klopstock was tolerably acute, but the solving thosehieroglyphical affairs, sent impaled by a .•liewer von a piece of beef by some butcher, is not easv, especially when grease and gravy have lent their charms to the dirty scrap of paper upon which tile legend relating to " lbs. B. M. or S." is scribbled. A greengrocer's bill,too, is rather puzzling, from the way in which this verdant t‘adestnan mixes up goose• terries and greens, ehubarb and red currants, while potatoes, parsnips and peas are all over the paper. Then there was the milkman, who invariable charged more pen'orths of milk than bed been tekea in—n specimen of dishonesty only surpassed by the baker, who always contrived to put crusty cottages in the bill that had never entered the door of the house in Briinswick.square. At least this was the opinion of Miss Klee, stock, who fully believed in a general trade conspire e to ruin the home of Mark Woolford, now that he was left alone and unprotected, and hence she felt. hereelf bound to throw her strong mind into the gap. To effectually carry this out, she used to shut herself up in a room by herself, and do battle with the various trade calculations, to come forth beaming with triumph if she could only find out a mistake in either of the bills. Certainly Mies Klopstock's time was not valuable, otherwise it might be questioned whether the expenditure at a whole evening to save the price or a half-quartern loaf was worth while. But it sati,tied the lady, and that was everything. Upon one of these occasions Ruth was left alene with Mark, busying herself with her work, but lookieg troubled and conscious; for, ceeainly. matters were growing worse in connection with Martin, who seemed now quite to shun the society of his brother. Mark made two or three observations to the gentle erl, but she answered so absently, and seemed in such trouble, that he ceased speaking after a time, and sat watching the pretty little white lingers, thet he told himself he was never to clap in love, busily weaving some kind of pattern from a ball of wool. "Ruth," he said, at last; and his words came so sudelenly that she let fall her work into her lap, and gazed at him nervously with parted lips. "Why, what a timid little bird it Ls!" he Bald, smiling. "Anyone would think that instead of being a brother—" _ _ _

Ruth's eyes brightened, and she darted at him on the instant a grateful look. That I was one of the ogres out of a story hook.' She smiled at him now, and his be,trt throbbed heavily; but he went on with enforced composure. " Come here, Ruth, dear. I want to talk t ) you seriously." Ruth rose, trembling as she placed the stool, to which he pointed, on the hearthrug, at his feet, and then Look up, as if to continue, her work. " Never mind the work now, my dear," he said, taking one of her hands in his, and patting it gently in the full strength of his vow to do his duty to bin brother, even to the end of the selt-sacrifice it might entail. _

Buth's head drooped lower and lower, and a deep Hush coloured her face while she fixed her eyes upon I;er work. it is not often we have a good, quiet chat together, my child," he said; "so as Miss Klopstock is busy, suppose we have one to-night. Ruth, my dear, I want to calk to you about money matters." She uttered a sigh of relief. The desire to snatch away her hand existed no longer, and, raising her face, the looked up timidly in his eyes. "About money, Mark? Yes?" she said. "You see, Ruth, my dear, I am taking up with you, not only the position of elder brother, but I feel that in my old-fashioned way I must be father as well."

'Deer Mark," she said, with the tears in her eyes, "I can never be sufficiently grateful." "Grateful, my char !" be said, kindly; "why your very presence here more than pays us for anything we could ever do for you. But come: this is to be a business chat, and we shall have Aunt Klopstock down directly to throw half-quartern loaves at icy devoted head, and recount the peccadilloes of the butcher's boy." Mark's attempts at joking were rather pondero us, but Ruth smiled, and he went on. - - -

"You see, Ruth, I've been thinking fl good deal about you lately." " About me, Mark!" she said, in alarm; and as he law the change, a pang shot through his breast. "Yes," he said, with a slight hoarseness in his voice, "about you, my child. You see you are quite II little heiress, and I want to do the best I van for you. There is an opening just now for a small sum of money to be invested in a certainty that I know will rosy excellent interest; and in the course of a few years grow far more profitable. You have just two hundred and ten pounds, inAuding the interest, and I have been thinking you shall sign a little note giving we the power to draw it. and I will buy the shares for you." "No, no," she said, hurriedly, "I cannot I—it is impossible. Oh, Mark, dear Mark, pray do not be angry with me." "Angry with you, my little bird?" he said in astonishment. "Of course not. It is your own to do with as you please. I only wished to increase it for you. How could I be angry with you if you preferred to keep it where it is? Perhaps it would be better there." "No, no; I don't mean that. I don't distrust you. Pray, pray, don't think that, Mark," she cried. piteously. "You, who are always so kind and thoughtful for me. Please do not think I distrust you. But I cannot—lcannot do what you say—about the money." 'Well, well." he said, gently, feeling puzzled the while at her strange burst of erxcitement. "It shall remain as you wish, my dear. I only thought that it would give you a few pounds more a year for pocket money." "Oh, Mark, Mark!" she cried, passionately, "I want you to believe in me and trust me. I cannot keep anything from you. I have not—l cannot do as you say—l have not got the money now !" Mark sat gazing down at her for the moment as if le had been stunned. Then his brow began to knit— Rot in anger but in pain, and he let fall the band he had caressed. _ . _
"You have not got the money ?" he said. "No," she said, catching his band in turn, and cling- ing to it. "Oh, Mark, pray, pray, do not be angry with me."

There was a dead silence for a few minutes, during which he at gazing down in her appealing face. "I am not angry with you, Ruth," he said, at last. "But tell me—dm I right? Has—has— Oh, surely Martin could not be such kt— Surely, my child, Martin has not persuaded you to let him invest this money r
"No, nor she laid, piteously. "Thank heaven!" said Mark, fervently.

"I—T— Oh, Mark, I must tell you all," she said, piteously. "You misunderstand me. I want to be silent. but I feel that I must tell you all." "Yes, my child; tell me ail," he said, gently. "God forbid, Ruth, that the day should ever come when you could not come to me as a friend—as a brother. Tell me, my dear ehild, tell me all." "It was some time ago, Mark, and Martin came to me in sore distress. fie had been led into some speculation by which he hoped to make a great deal of money, and he had been within a hairbreadth of making quite a fortun- when all went wrong, and he had a hundred pounds to pay." "Yes," said Mark, with a little s;sh. "Go on."

, "Re came to me and told me that if the money was not paid the result would be disgrace and dishonour. How could I do other than give him the money—to the son of her who had been almost more than mother to me?'

There was again a dead silence, and Mark's face grew more deeply lined. "That was some time back?' he said at last. "And the rest?" "That is not long ago," she replied. "Poor fellow. he made frantic efforts to recover what he had lost for my sake, he said; and he told me that he could wot endure the feeling of obligation to me." "And he—speculated again, Ruth?' said Mark, quietly. "Yes, Mark.* "Ind lost ?"

"And lost, Marks Oh, it was so grievous— so piteous to see his sufferings. He told me what h.rl happened, but he did not ask me to help him. I had to beg of him to take the money, Mark—l had, indeed, I don't think he would have taken it if I had not pressed him very, very hard. But why do you laugh?" "Did I laugh ?" he said, sadly. "It was nothing.' "He is going to pay it all back to me, Mark." "Yes, so I suppose,', replied Mark, taking her head between his hands, and kissing her forehead reverently, and then gazing in her sweet, candid eyes.

The report to the Committee of the House of Commons of the Local Government Board on the W:irrington Extension, Water, and ,Improvement Bill. 1890, has just been received by the Town Clerk of Warrington (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle). The Board state with regard to the recital of the Bill that it Icexpedient that the boundaries of the existing lborough should be extended in the manner men* tioned by the Bill, the instruction of the House of Commons to the Committee ofi the Bill that no pro- visions should be assented to that should have the result of the borough being situated in more than one administrative counts rendered it unnecessary for the Board to refer to the manifold difficulties Ithat would arise if the proposals of the Corpora- tion, as embodied in the Bill, with reference to the I extension of the borough, were assented to, and no i I alteration were made n the county boundary. In connection with the proposed extension, the Board thought it right to draw the attention of the Cor- poration to provisions of the Local Government Act, 1888, which enabled the Board by provisional order, on the representation of the Council of any county oi borough, after local inquiry, to alter the area of any county or borough. The Corporation would no doubt inform the Com- mittee of the measures which, in their opinion, had rendered it desitable that the extension of. the borough should be effected by means of a private bill instead of having a Provisional Order under the Act named. With regard to the proposed pur- chase of the Waterworks, the Board said that it was to be Write in mind that the putchase was, under the ilh, proposed to be made, -in default of agree- ment, compulsorily, upon terms to be. fixed in case of dispute by arbitration, and that consequently , neither the Corporation nor the Committee had the same opportunity of estimating the probable finan- cial result of the purchase as they would have if the price of the undertaking had been ascertained. Under these circumstances it appeared to the Board that the Committee would require to be furnished with strong evidence of the advantages likely to result from the acquisition of the undertaking by the Corporation before they authorised its compul- sory purchase as proposed by the Bill. The resolu- tion of the Town Council to promote the Bill had not received the approval of the Board as recited. Dealing in detail with the Bill, the Board say, with regard to the proposed extension, that so far as appears from the first schedule to the Bill part of the proposed borough boundary follows imaginary lines. In the second part of the schedule there are several references to the Manches- ter Ship Canal and works in connection therewith, intended to be constructed or now in course of construction. The Board suggest, for the consideration of the Committee, whether it is desirable to fix the boundary of the Borough by references to works not yet completed, and of which the position may vary within the limits of deviation. After observations on "Authority of Corporation extended," "charters and bye-laws to apply to extended borough." and " exemption from liability to certain rates and collection of arrears," the report refers at some length to the Water Works question, referring the Committee to the observations on the preamble of the Bill. Observations are also offered on the clauses dealing with infectious diseases, buildings, streets, sanitary provisions, hackney carriages, and other matters dealt with in the Bill. Speaking of clause 161, which relates to the limit of the library rate being extended, the Board point out that the Kingston- upon-Thames Improvement Act, 1888, contains a provision that the rate shall not be increased beyond the sum of one penny in the pound, without the consent of the burgesses of the borough, to be expressed in the same manner as is provided by the Public Libraries' Act, 1855, with reference to the adoption thereof. In regard to clause 177,—" repeal of section 37 of the Gas Act, 1877, relating to the redemption of annuities "—the Board do not object to the principle of the clause, but suggest that if it is allowed by the Committee, some alteration should be made in the mode of applying the sinking fund for the redemption of the annuities.

THE PROPOSED PURCHASE OF THE WATER WORKS. On Monday a meeting of the General Purposes Committee was held at the Town Hall, the Mayor in the chair, to further consider the proposed pur- chase of the Water Works. It was decided to en- gage an eminent water engineer to advise the Cor- poration as to the likelihood of the Winwick water supply being permanent, and to supply other information he may deem necessary before the purchase is concluded.

div.head: OPPOSITION.
div.p: THE OPPOSITION.

A case had been set down for hearing by the promoters of the Warrington Extension and Water Bill to dispute the locus standi of the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited, in oppos- ing the Bill before Committee in the House of Commons, but it has been postponed. It is not likely that there will be any difficulty on this head, now that the Corporation have come to terms with the firms using the river water. The prospects of the Bill may thus far be regarded as favourable to its becoming law.

div.head: DEATH OF AN OLD TRADESMAN.
div.p: DEATH OF AN OLD TRADESMAN.

On Saturday night, Mr. Thos. Craik, an old an respected bookseller and stationer, of Church-street, St. Helens, and a native of Warrington, died at his residence in Knowsley-road, St. Helens. The deceased gentleman had been ailing for about eight years past, but was, until recently, able to go about. In August last he paid a visit to his son, Mr. Joseph H. Craik, town clerk of Batley, and formerly deputy . town clerk of St. Helens, and while there he was taken seri- ously ill. He remained at Batley for two months, and his condition having then much improved, he returned home. However, he never appears to have thoroughly recovered, and about a week before his death he was obliged to take to his bed, and despite every care and attendance by Drs. Gaskell and Jackson, he suc- cumbed on Saturday night, to the great regret of a large circle of friends. He died at the age of sixty- four years. Mr. Craik was one of the oldest St. Helens tradesmen. He was a native of Warrington, and came to St. Helens in June. 1853. He occupied a position in the shop of Mr. Isaac Sharp, bookseller and stationer, Old Market Place,until that gentleman's death, and then he commenced business on his own account as a bookseller and stationer, in Church-st., close to the Parish Church. Here he lived for several years, and then re- moved to Old Market Place, subsequently again removing to Church-st., but, in the meantime, in 1874, he had taken up his residence at "The Homestead," Knowsley-road, where he died as stated. Although Mr. Craik did not take any active part in public affairs, he took a great interest in them, no doubt on account of both his sons occupying positions in the town clerk's office. He was a staunch Churchman and a Liberal in politics,and was for many years the.local agent for the British and Foreign Bible Society. He leaves behind a widow and three chil- dren—Mr. Joseph Hanson Craik, town-clerk of Batley; Mr. Thomas Crtik, of the town-clerk's department, St. Helens ; andltissCraik, whci has carried on her father's ' business. The remains were interred at Windle Cemetery, st. Helens, on Thursday afternoon.

div.head: WELSH COLLIERY FLOODED.
div.p: A WELSH COLLIERY FLOODED.

Another outburst of water at the Albion Colliery, Pontypridd, was on Thursday reported. Three miners were working in No. 2 pit at the time of the crush, one of whom, John Morgan, a married man, was drovrned. The other men were rescued before the mine ' was flooded.

div.head: TUE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 3, 1890,
div.p: TUE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MAY 3, 1890,
A SHIP CANAL LECTURE.
THE SHIP CANAL BRIDGES AT LATCHFCIID

REETING DARESBORY HIGHWAY BOARD., On Wednesday a special meeting of the Daresbury Highway Board was held at Daresbury "for the purpose of considering proposals of the Blanchester Ship Canal Company in respect of the highways at Appleton, Grappenhall, and Latchford." The chair was taken by Mr. Cliffe, the vice-president, and there was a fair attendance of members. Mr. Leader Williams was prelent on behalf of the Canal Com- pany. A letter was read from the solicitors to the Manchester Ship Canal Company (Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw and Co.) in regard to the Company's vari- ous Powers Bill now before tho Committee of the Rouse of Commons. In it they stated that the Cheshire County Council, and the London and North-Western Railway Company declined to accept the arrangements shown on the plans de- posited by the Company with reference to the pro- posed road deviations and new roads in Latchford In consequence of this the Company would have no alternative but to withdraw the. part of the Bill, including the works in connection with the Northwich and Warrington-road, unless some settlement could be arrived at. The County Council and the London and North-Western Railway. Company had expressed them- selves willing to modify their opposition, if the Canal Company would convert the proposed foot bridge at Latchford station into a high level traffic bridge, but the Company could not do this unless the Highway Board would consent to the closing of Ackers-lane and the giv- ing up of the swing bridge over the canal there. The Canal Company, therefore, asked the Highway Board to do this, and if it were done the company would make a connection road from Ackers-lane to the high level bridge.—ln supporting the proposal of the company, Mr. LEADER WILLIAMS pointed out that the Highway Board with the concurrence of Mr. Stanhope Bull, the Cheshire county surveyor, had agreed to the removal of the pro- posed swing bridge over Knutsford-rd. being removed about 100 yards to the west so as to take the place of both the Knutsford-rd. and the Grappenhall-rd. swing bridges.—Mr. J. C. PARR remarked that Mr. Bull had no official authority to modify the original plans.—Mr. WILLIAMS said the Canal Company were quite willing to carry out the agreement to alter the locality of Knuts- ford-road bridge, but they now found that the Cheshire County Council, which had power over Knutsford-road, absolutely declined to allow them t removethe bridgeto the point suggested by Mr. Bull. The question was now, therefore, whether the Highway Board would agree to the abandonment of the Ackers-lane swing bridge on condition that a high level vehicular bridge be constructed near Latchford station. The Canal Company would, how- ever, decline to make the high level bridge for the County Council and the London and North-Western Railway Company unless the Highway Board agreed to the doing away with Ackers-lane swing bridge.—Mr. Williams having retired from the Board room,a consider- able amount of discussion took place as to the proposal that had been made. It was pointed out by some of the members that it was almost exactly the same as the Proposals that had been before the Board on two or three previousoccasions and rejected. It was also remarked that if the Highway Board again rejected the offer the Canal Company would probably have to go back to their original plans which include a swing bridge for both Knutsford-road and Grappenhall-road. Mr. Lona thought it would be better if the original plan of the Knutsford-road bridge was carried out. The alterations would inconvenience people from Lymm and Thelwall who ought to have consideration as well as those in the district of that authority. (Hear, hear.)—Some further conversation showed that there was still a strong opinion on the Board in favour of the retention of Ackers- lane swing bridge, though Mr. J. C. PARR was of opinion that a high level bridge would prevent all the inconveni- ence of waiting that would be experienced when vessels were passing the swing bridges, which might in some cases be as long as sixteen or twenty minutes.—The CLERK pointed out that the swing bridges would not need to be opened for barges, but only for the large vessels which would come up on the tides.—Mr. W. PIERPOINT referred to the disadvantages of a high level goods station at Latchford, and said if such a station were made he should make arrangements for the carting of his traffic to Warrington.—Mr. LONG did not think a high level station at Latchford would be much used either for goods or by passengers. Nor did he think that a high level vehicular bridge over the canal would be much used owing to the steepness of the gradients.—Mr. W. PIERPOINT proposed" that this Board can only agree to the high level bridge on condition that the Ackers- lane bridge is retained."—Mr. T. HALL seconded this pro- posal which was agreed to.—Mr. LEADER WILLIAMS was then called into the room and informed of the decision of the Board. He said that under these circumstances he should have to recommend his directors to withdraw the proposals. He was sorry the Board had adopted the course they had, and he thought that in the future they viould regret not having accepted a high level swing bridge.—Mr. Lona said the Board did not wish to throw unnecessary opposition in the way of the Canal Corn- pany, but they had to consider theinterests of all parties. —Mr. WILLIAMS acknowledged the kindness of the Board.—The meeting then terminated.

WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH.

The parochial report for the period during Easter 1889 to Easter 1890, just issued, gives some interest- ing particulars of the work carried on in connection with this eh arch. Early in the year the ladies of the congregation subscribed £37 ss. 2d. for the purpose of beautifying the East End of the Church, and of this sum .f.. 3- was expended in an altar 'frontal, leaving a balance in hand ss. 2d. Two anonymous friends presented a new altar and Re- Table at a cost of £25, and two other friends pre- sented two pairs of valuable brass flower vases. A brass Altar Cross and Velyq Dossal had been placed in the church at the cost of 1116 9s. 3d., the volun- tary contributions of members of the congregation, collected by Mrs. Woods. Oak cupboards for the use of the choir were placed in church, new kneelers in some of the free sittings, and certain alterations in the others, were effected at a cost of £27. The organ had been cleaned, renovated, and in some respects reconstructed at a cost of £l2O. The number of communicants had increased rapidly, especially on Easter day, when it was about double that of the preceding year. The late Mr. James Morris bequeathed to the parish alegacy of £l,OOO with the request that the balance, after paying legacy duty and expending £lOO in a painted window, should be invested and allowed to accummulate untiiit amounted to £l,OOO, when it was to be applied to the use of the poor. Accordingly the small window in South Gallery had been filled with stained glass to the memory of Mr. Morris, and the balance of money invested by the execu- tors. An Assistant Clergy Fund had been started, which it is hoped will amount to £3OO yearly, apportioned as follows ; (1) £lOO paid by the Committee of the Clergy Daughters' School, for duties of chaplain performed ; (2) £lOO from the voluntary subscriptions of friends (of this £BO per annum for five years has been promised) and (3) £lOO yearly from the offertories made in Church. A Parochial Missionary Association had been formed, and for its first definite work had made itself responsible for a bell for the Cathedral Church at Peking. The Rev. C. E. Jackson was requested by the Bishop to ' act as Secretary. In addition to other work the Parochial Clergy have initiated some useful work among the Blind Poor : (1) A Home Teaching Society which provides Elementary Teaching in Reading and Writing for the Blind. and (2) Work,hops for Teaching the more active Blind Men a handicraft. A permanent Lending Library of 70 volumes has also been established. To do this work subsCriptions of about £l7O have been obtained. An unoccupied house near the church gates was rented in November, 1888, by the Rector, at a yearly rent of £lO. One small room has been used for a Parish Room, one other, together with a third constructed at the Rector's expense out of an outhouse and a cellar, has been regularly used for iittrochial work. The statement regarding the schools in clnnection with the church gives the following particulars as to the number 'of scholars on the books : —Church-st. Boys' School 250, Mount Girls' School 260, Crossley-st School 279, Bank-st. School 170, and Orford Barracks School 60. A bible class for women has been commenced in Smith-st. by Mrs. Willis, and has a membership of 100, with an aver- age attendance of 60. Other bible classes have been organised, and among other useful institutions are a day nursery, a sick and burial society, and a penny bank and clothing club. At the latter the sum of £560 wa.s paid in by 900 depositors. SERMONS ON SUNDAY.

In his sermon at the Parish Church, on Sunday even- ing, the Rev. C. E. Jackson (curate) referred to the parochial work of the past year. In matters clerical, ecclesiastical, educational, ministerial, charitable, and missionary, the work in that parish had cost £5,400. Of that sum £1,750 was voluntary offerings ; 1,514 children were taught in the day schools ; and 1,100 in Sunday schools. There was a small army of Sunday school teachers and other fellow-workers with the clergy; and in the mothers' meetings and sewing classes there were over 500 members. That implied a vast amount of voluntary work and sacrifice Had their part .been duly fulfilled? The fabric must be pre- served against decay and the ravages of time. There was the cleaning, the heating, the lighting, the cost of music and choir, and the preparatiorr of seats. There was the service of the ministers. Until they had made some adequate discharge, accerding to their ability, of this common ordinary just debt, there was no question of offering to God or sacrifice. The offerings made last year seemed large, but the givers did not miss them. Let them make a resolution to double them this year. Let those who gave a halfpenny give a penny; let those who gave a penny give twopence. It was a possible and a practicable vow, and many, he was sure, would make it. The Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) referred to the same subject in his sermon in the morning. From the report issued of the work done ..luring 1889 and 1890, he said the congregation would see that a sum of £1,802 Os. 4itl. had been given, but besides £BOO had been allotted the church from Sir Gilbert Greenall's Jubilee gift, and £l,OOO bequeathed to the parish by a late parishioner. of the £1,802 about £1,500 belonged to the Parish Church, and there was about £lOO each for the Bank-st and Crossley-st. Missions. Roughly speaking, £5OO of the £l,BOO had been given in the offertory, and the re- mainder had been subscribed for special purposes. How- ever ungracious it might seem, ft,r the future he had to ask more. The £5OO given in the offertory last year was not sufficient for the efficient maintenance of the church, and he earnestly trusted that during the current year the offertory would reach the sum of £7OO. They proposed . to have forty ordinary collections and twelve special. By the former they hoped to raise £lO per Sunday, and at each of eleven out of the special services they hoped to realize £l5. On the occasion of the harvest festival

it was hoped to obtain about £BO. The Rector then went on to enumerate the special objects which needed Support from the offertory, and lastly mentioned that there was the Additional Clergy Fund, towards which he himself gave £300; £lOO came from services he ren- dered to the Clergy Daughters' School. £BO per year was promised by outside friends, and the officers of the qhurch had promised to give £lOO from the offertory. He appealed to all present to give according to their means, and asked them to give ungrudgingly.

div.head: AFRICA AND ITS PEOPLE..
div.p: AFRICA AND ITS PEOPLE..

On Tuesday evening Mr. George Manning gave a very interesting lecture in the large coffee-room on the Ship Canal Works, at Morrisbrook, Thelwall, be- fore a fair audience. The lecture, which was, as a matter of fact, several lectures condensed into one, was 'very fluently delivered, and dealkiwith Africa, its people, and its manufactures, a subject with which Mr. Manning is very familar, and in regerd to which he has for a considerable number of years taken a deep interest. The chair was taken by Mr. Ewart, who stated that the proceeds would be given towards providing funds to enable the day school children to have a trip to the seaside. At the present time, he added, Africa was in the minds of most people, and it would be very interesting to hear about that country. He was sure that Mr. Manning would tell them some- thing that was worth listening to. (hear, hear.) Mr. Manning said that it was forty years since he conceived the idea of taking up Africa as a matter of study. Let him in the first place say that, although they had a smaller attendance than had been expected, the funds of the school would• not suffer very much, as he should be able to hand over £3 or £4 that had been sent him by friends on behalf of the trip. With what had been received for tickets he had, no doubt, they would have sufficient money to carry out the object in view. Africa, he continued, was looked upon by certain nationalities with an eager eye, and there was new a general scramble on the part of certain nations for the territory that used to be called" No man's land." Africa used to be called a continent, but it was to all intents and purposes an island. The Suez Canal was the opening up of an ancient waterway, thereby connecting the Red Sea with the Mediterranean. It was accepted by scien- tific men that the Soudan, the Mediterranean Sea, and right away up to the Baltic, was one vast in- land fresh water sea, and that -the waters had subsided from the Soudan, leaving that arid desert which was nearly as large as Europe. One reason assigned for this supposition was that on the shores of the Baltic, on the shores of the Mediterranean, in the Jordan Valley, and in c&tain parts of Eastern Soudan, the same flowers, and fossils of corresponding appearance were found. It had been an unfortunate matter for African affairs that on that deadly coast, full of poison- ous malaria, the brighest and the best of England's sons had been lost in the endeavour to bring to our knowledge what we now know of the interior of Africa. Having spoken of the geographical characteristics of Africa, the lecturer referred to its dense forests, to the roads, the war paths, the slave paths, and said that Africa might be divided into three parts--the north for health, the south for commerce, and the centre for enterprise and discovery. In the opening up of Central Africa it was a pleasure to mention that England and the world would long be debtors to the "African Lakes Company" and the East African Company," for the work which for years they here pursued, at a great outlay, on behalf of civilisation. The climate was varied—from the snow- capped mountains to equatorial heat. In Africa there were many nations and tribes, some with names and some without, and 2,000 dialects and languages. They were said to be a lazy people, but the abundance of natural products relieved them from the necessity of work. But that they could work was shown by the fact of the opening up of roads. under the •direction of travellers. They wee a prey to the slave hunters. It was computed that in Central Africa alone, an area of 35,000 miles, there was not long since a population of one million. That population had now ceased. The old markets of • Africa, still open, were the Cape in the south, the West Coast, Egypt, and the Nile Valley. The new markets would be amongst those who lived near the waterways, the roads, and the forests, where, to some extent markets were already held. The first necessity in Africa was the establishment of a military authority strong enough to put down the slave hunter, to enforce justice, equity, and freedom, to protect the, natives, guard the roads, ensure safe transit, and to assist commercial and phil- anthropic enterprise. Another necessity was the em- ployment of capital, scientific and skilled labour' and unskilled labour. England was the nation that had these attributes' and her civilising influence was being felt in Africa. For that country he saw a brighter day, and he saw a brighter day for England, with new mar- kets, and with new homes for her sons and daughters.

• LETTER FROM STANLEY. Mr. Manning recently wrote to Mr. H. M. Stanley congratulating him upon his discoveries, and stating how deeply interisted he had been for the last forty years in African matters. He also mentioned that he was about to give a lecture on Africa in aid of a fund for sending some of the Ship Canal children to the seaside. In reply Mr. Manning has received the following letter : Palais du Bruselles, 24th April.

My Dear Sir,-1 am obliged by your letter of the 18th, and in reply have to say that the average height of the dwarfs we met is a little over four feet, but of course some are taller thanothers, the same as other nations. My time is so fully occupied that I cannot spare the time to give you any further information, but you will find all par- ticulars about them in thy forthcoming work, which will be published in a few weeks. With best wishes for the success of your lecture,—l am, dear sir, yours very truly' HENRY M. STANLEY.
