div.head: LIFTROT CHARITY OF RUNCORN.
div.p: THE LIFTROT CHARITY OF RUNCORN.

At the adjourned meeting of the ratepayers of Runcorn last week a discussion, arose on the sub- ject of this charity and a communication from the secretary, Mr. W. Fisher, who stated that the trusteerwere of opinion that they were not under any obligation to render accounts to the church- wardens. Mr. W. Handley, whose researches ,into the charities of the district have caused' Such widespread interest, contended that there was nothing in the scheme of the charity which showed that the charity was outside the Act of Parliament which required the accounts of parochial or en- dlwed charities to be presented at the annual vestry meeting. He then read the scheme of the charity, of which he had obtained an official copy, and as it is the richest charity in the township and of eonsiderable antiquity we give particulars :

The scheme states that the Charity Commissioners for England and Wales having considered an applicatiop : made to them on the 14th day of December, 18851. in the i matter of the charity of Liptrot and others, by the Rev. John Barclay. vicar of the Parish of Runcorn, the Rev. ' George Bright Bennett, incumbent of the District Church 1, of Holy Trinity at Runcorn, and John Linaker Wright, Wm. Wright, and Robert Cheshyre Whiteway, all of ' Runcorn,being the present acting trustees of the charity; and it appearing to the Board of Charity Commissioners that the endowment of the charity consists of a close of , land situated in Runcorn, and containing 2 acres, 23 , perches, or thereabouts, which was demised by an : indenture, dated 21st day of April, 1864, to James Rigby, I for a term of 999 years from 20th December 1863, at the I yearly rent of £64 175., and that the gross annual income of the said charity exceeds £5O, and that it is for the ' advantage of the said charity that a scheme for its future 1 administration should be established in a manner here- after mentioned, the Board do hereby order that the scheme contained and set forth in the schedule hereto be , approved and established as the scheme for the future regulation and management of the above mentioned charity. The scheme thus alluded to is as follows (1.) The vicar of the parish of Runcorn and the perpetual curate or incumbent of the district church of the Holy Trinity, Runcorn, and their respec- tive successors ft the time being, and three other respectable persons resident in the same parish, or 1 within the distance of seven miles from the church there- of shall be the trustees of the charity. (2.) Any trustee of charity (not being a trustee by virtue of his office), ' who shall become bankrupt or insolvent or incapacitated to act, or who shall cease to be resident in the said parish or within the distance of seven miles from the church thereof, or who shall not attend any meeting of the trustees during a consecutive period of two years, shall in any such cases immediately cease to be a trustee, and thereupon, or upon the death or resignation of any such trustee, a new trustee qualified as aforesaid shall be ap- pointed by the other trustees at their first meeting, which shall be held after the lapse of one calendar month next after the occurrence of such vacancy by a resolution to be forthwith notified by them, with all proper informa- tion, to the Charity Commissioners for England and Wales, at their office in London, but no such appoint- ment shall be valid until the same shall have been , ap- proved by the said Commissioners and their approval certified under their official seal. (3.) The trustees shall hold meetings in some convenient place within the parish, as often as may be found necessary for the man- , agement of the charity and at least twice in each year, on the first Wednesday in March, and the first Wednesday in September. The Incumbent, if pre- ] sent, or, in his absence, the senior trustee present . according to the date or order of his appointment, . shall be the chairman at every meeting. Three trustees shall form a quorum at any meeting. Any two trustees may summon a special meeting giving ten days' previous notice in writing to the other trustees, and specifying in such notice the object of such meeting. All matters and questions shall be determined by the majority of the trustees present at any meeting, and in the case of 'equality of votes, the Chairman shall have a double or I casting vote. (4.) A minute book and proper books of account shall be provided by the trustees, and kept in , some convenient and secure place of deposit to be pro- vided or appointed by them for that purpose, and I minutes of the entry into office or the appointment of 1 every new trustee and of all proceedings of the trustees, shall be entered in such minute book and signed by the Chairman at the termination of the proceedings at each meeting. (5.) Full accounts shall be kept of the receipts and expenditure of the trustees in respect of the charity, in the books to be provided for that purpose; and such accounts shall be examined and passed annually at the March meeting and signed by the trustees then present. (6.) The trustees shall be at liberty, if they think fit, to appoint and employ a person as clerk and treasurer, or in either of those offices, at an annual svlletry not exceeding £5 to be paid out of the 1 income of the charity, and such person shall keep the accounts ef the charity and shall teceive the rents ara.2 liicoine ail,4. Make the several payments thereout, under the immediate io- ilezol snd superintendence of the trustees, who shall be responsLi4.! for thQ-Ctr ,aPPIiC4- tion by him of all such moneys, or he shall discniiitl'u such of the said duties as shall be required of him by the trustees. (7) All the estates and property ef the charity, not required to be retained or occupied for the purposes thereof, shall be let and otherwise managed by the trustees, who shall receive all the rents and annual and other income ; and in every case a sufficient public notice of the intention to let any land or property shall be given by the trustees in the said township of Run- corn, and also in any different parish or parishes in which such land or property shall be situate, in such manner as they shall consider most effectual for giving full publicity to such intention. (8) Any money arising from the sale of thnber or from any mines or minerals on the charity estate, shall be treated as capital and in- vested in the Government funds, in the name of the official trustees of charitable funds in trust for the charity, except in any special cases in which the trustees may be authorized by the Charity Commissioners for England and Wales to apply such money or any part thereof to income. (9) The trustees shall be at liberty to appropriate and apply out of the clear annual income of the charity the sum of £25 towards the benefit and support of a r school or schools for the instruction and education of the children of labourers and other persons of the poorer class residing in the said township of Runcorn as long as such school or schools shall be efficiently and properly conducted, and there shall not be any rule or practice in the management thereof, which shall operate to exclude any children, being Christians, from admission thereto upon the sole ground of their particular religions creed or persuasion, and the remainder ef such income, shall be applied by the said trustees to the benefit of the most deserving and necessitous inhabitants of the said town- ship of Runcorn to be selected for this purpose by the trustees, by providing them with clothes, bedding, fuel, medical or other aid in sickness, food or other articles in kind, or with pecuniary aid in special cases, as shall be considered by the trustees to be most advantageous to them, and that either directly or by aiding the funds of any provident or friendly associations to which they shall belong, or any public institution, of which respectively, it shall be the object to provide them with like benefits and so that no funds of the charity shall be applied directly or indirectly to the re.ief of the poor rates of the said parish. (10.) If any doubt or ques- tionshall arise amongst the trustees or any of' them as to the construction or proper application of any of the provisions of the scheme or the mknagement of the charity, application shall be made by them to the Charity Commissioners for England and Wales for their opinion and advice; which when given shalt be conclusive. The scheme was sealed by order of the Board on the 6th day of March, HU, and was signed by Henry M. Vane, secretary. ' Although the trustees decline to furnish copies of the accounts to the vestry meeting, they have courteously announced that any ratepayer is at liberty to examine them on application to the secretary, and on Tuesday, our representative paid a visit to that gentleman's office. Mr. W. Fisher very readily disclosed the balance sheet to the inspection of his visitor; from which it appeared that the income was made up as follows :-Balance from , last year £3O is. ; to one years rent of land from Samuel White, £64 17s. ; total receipts £94 las. The expendi- ture was as follows : For bread, £1 ; to poor af Runcorn (not belonging), £34- 2s. 6d. ; paid to sundry applicants, £3 9s. 8(1.; to treasurer of National School, £10; to treasurer of Holy Trinity School, £10; to Newtown Mission School, £5; to secretary, £2; allowed Samuel White, income tax on £64 if., n. /2s. 6cl : balance in hands of treasurer £27 13s. 4(1, total £94 18s. The money distributed was given to 135 persons, who each received ss. The payment to "sundry applicants" was made up as follows: Three poor persons, ss. each ; Rev. W. Preston, £1 7s. 4-d.; Tcwns Nurse Fund, £1 7s. 4(1. Our readers have thus an opportunity of seeing how the funds are spent by the trustees, who are, the Rev. A. M. Wood, vicar; Rev. Dr. Pieston. Messm F. A. Lake, E. Timmins, and John Ttrundrit. Mr. Fisher also placed . before our representative the accounts of the Alcotk and Poors Field Charity, which showed that the incomQ for 1889 was made up as follows :-Balance from last year, £3 13s. 90. ; Mr. Robert Dopler, rent of poor's field, £7: amount received from charity commissioners on account of Allcock Charity tper Rev. A. Maitland Wood), £3 is. Bd.; total, £l3 15s. sd. The payments were made to poor of Runcorn (not belonging) £3 10s.; to executors of late Peter Briscoe for bread, £4 4s. ; balance in hand £O3 is. 5d., total £l3 158. &d. Fourteen persons received the sum of ss. each.

Houghton, Kilshaw, Smith, Kilshall, Ileaton, Swinton, Warburton, Owen, A. Jolley; S. Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sephton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (nuisance inspector.) Chamberlain TILE Government Bill for the set- and the Cement of the land question in Ire- Land Bill, land has been further discussed by the House of Commons during the past week; and the more it is discussed the more obvious it ap- pears that, instead of doing any good, it is likely to make bad worse. It is a serio is matter for Parliament to impose a scheme of land purchase upon the people of Ireland in utter opposition to the wishes of the representatives of Ireland. How can it possibly come to good if the local credit of the country is swallowed up in a measure which the country does not want? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN has strained his convictions again and again in order to keep the present Ministry in power. He is straining them at the present time ; but he fore- sees that the bill, if passed as it stands, will prove a failure, and he is careful not to commit his to it as a whole. He spoke at some length on the subject in the House on Monday night; but he had very little to say in support of the Bill. Indeed, the greater portion of his speech was occupied in discussing the scheme pro- pounded by Mr. PARNELL, and in showing that it might, in part at least, be dove-tailed into the present measure. The Tories looked to the mem- ber for 'West Birmingham to back their Bill through thick and thin. It was, therefore, a bitter pill for them to find that he had very little to say about it, and that what he did say was in the nature of an admission that it could only be made acceptable in connection with a scheme of Local Self-Government. Mr.-CHAMBERLAIN says : I would ask the Government whether it would not be possible to give an assurance that the County Councils which will be estaolished in their Bill should have a voice in the negotiations which take place in regard to the transfer of land, and have a veto in these transactions, and shall have an interest in their success, and shall become the landlord, and pay over to the British Exchequer that portion of the rents which are to be paid back in instalments. It will be interesting to see whether the Govern- ment pledge themselves to what is, after all, a species of Home Rule; but, even if they do, we submit that it is not the right way to go to work. The Local Government Bill should be dealt with first; for it is a case of trying to sell the pig in the poke to say —" We grant that the Land Bill is defective with no local authority behind it; but it will be all right when the Local Government Bill is passed." It was not in this lame and impotent way that Mr. GLADSTONE proceeded; he faced each and every issue by letting Parliament have two Bills before it—a dome Rule Bill and an Irish Land Bill. This was honest, straight-forward, statesman-like. MT. CHAMBERLAIN evidently feels that in this re- spect the situation has changed for the worse. He perceives that his new friends are putting the cart before the horse; and he is giving them what he regards as timely warning that they are not mov- ing on right lines. It is true that he tries to let the Government down gently; but he does let them down. Referring to the way in which it is pro- posed in the Bill to mortgage the local resources of Ireland he said : There is one other point which is of very much greater import ance —the objection that hon. members took to the hypothecation of the resources of the local authorities without their consent. (Hear, hear.) I think the Government themselves will admit that was a very strong thing to do. You hare only to test it by applying it to England and Scot Ictid. (hear, hear.) West would be said if you were to mortgage in any way the resources of the great municipalities of Great Britain without

consulting them as to the employment of the funds.. (dear, hear). I don't hesitate to say there would: be a very pretty kettle of fish. (Laughter) k- admit, therefore, that the objection of the hon meinb,d• impresses me most strongly. It is every" serious objection, and coupled with it comes the objection of the member for Midlothian, whose second or third vital objection was that we were' putting this country into the position of a State- landlord. I agree that if you put the British' Government into direct communication with Irish tenant, and make the Government the Teal collector, at all events you are paving the waY fo very considerable friction and irritation, ant' possibly even of danger. (Hear, hear.) Friction, irritation, danger—these are to be the- fruits of the Land Bill which the Government by mea,ns of their mechanical majority are forcing: through Parliament. The fact is the Ministry.are" unequal to the task they have set themselves; but ' they may do irreparable mischief, and meetings- ought to be held throughout the country to Pre"' test against this bungling bill. • Bali

IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE, WIDNES. A meeting of the members of the Widnes branch, was held in the League-rooms, on Sunday. Mr. J. William- son presided and an address was given by Mr. Daniel Boyle, organiser of the Lancashire branch. In advocacy of the claims of the League on Irishmen Mr. Boyle intends to make a house to house canvass of Widnes with the object of increasing the membership of the local branch of the League.

Interesting read- ings were given by Messrs. Wesley Cooke, Daniel Eisbrown, and Edward Key. Messrs. Thomas Heesom, James Johnson, and T. Whyte also took part in the meeting. J. Mad- den. There was a capital attendance. GARDEN Too.—J. B. Garland. Ironmonger, Warrington & Harlestown.

div.p: THE BURGLARIES ILT WIDNES.

On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Henry Hall, Pol- lard-st., Liverpool, and Edward Houghton, 89 Charter- street, Manchester, were charged on remand with burglariously entering the dwelling-house and shop of D. J. Brookes, tailor and outfitter, Victoria-road, and steal- ing therefrom a quantity of wearing apparel worth £8 12s. 7d. The evidence given at the former hearing was repeated, and showed that on Sunday the 20th inst., Mr. and Mrs. Brooke left home at noon leaving the ser- vant in charge of the house and children. At nine o'clock the servant securely fastened the door and retired to rest. At half-past ten Mr. and Mrs. Brookes returned home, and the former seeing a light in the kitchen, and hearing a scuffle in the yard he went there. He saw a man on the wall and another attempting to scale the wall, and at once attracted the attention of P.S. Laing and P.C. Hudson by blowing a whistle in his possession. The former saw Hall dropping from some hoardiwg into Victoria-road and he chased and captured the thief. After securing him in the police station he returned to Mr. Brookes establishment, and found Houghton con- cealed in an outhouse. The prisoners were wearing the I stolen clothing and had also enjoyed themselves amongst the eatables in the pantry. The prisoners it was traced, had effected an entrance by climbing up the water spout to the roof, where they, had removed some slates and broken through the ceiling into the workroom on the third floor. The prisoners, who made no reply to the charge, were committed to the Assizes for trial. The prisoners were further charged with having some time between the 19th and 21st broken into the lock-up shop of Thomas Carney, grocer and provision dealer, Water- loo-road. The shop was securely fastened on Saturday night, and on Monday morning Mr. Carney found that an entrance had been effected through a second storey window at the rear of the premises, and a desk had been forced open and 2s. taken out. The marks on the desk corresponded with a chisel found on Mr. Brookes pre- mises and presumedto belong to the prisoners, who were committed for trial on this charge also. SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fathiml9.—J. &W. DUTTON, 16 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. CHARITY FOOTBALL MATCH AT RI7NCORN. About 6,000 persons assembled on the field of the Runcorn Football Club, on Wednesday evening, to wit- ness a matth between the local team and Mr. Valentine's Lancashire team. The game had been arranged with the purpose of aiding the district Nurse Fund, towards' which the proceeds wig be devoted. The large assemb- lage included numerous persons of the gentler sex, of whom many had no doubt been attracted by the adver- tised novelty of a lady appearing in the football arena. As nursing is pre-eminently a woman's Office, it was thought that it would be very appropriate if a lady would start the game by " kicking off' the ball, and Miss Bertha Speakman, daughter of Mr. P. Speakman C.C., after some pressure, yielded to the request of those interested and consented to perform this duty. As she walked across the field to the centre escorted by Mr. Speakman, she was greeted with loud applause. The players formed a group, and Mr. Speakman in a brief speech referred in suitable terms to the object of the match, and thanked the visitors for their kindness in travelling to Runcorn and giving their services. Amid loud cheers, Miss Speakman then gave the ball a capital kick, and the game at once commenced fast and furious Play was very open, and the passing, especially by the home team was very fine indeed. Crompton, Davies and Hugh Hughes made many fine runs for Runcorn, and on the other side Valentine and Winterbottom, were very conspicuous. Crompton was the most succ6sful player, scoring a try, and dropping a goat in his customary cool manner. Unfortunately Davies was rather seriously injured about a quarter of an hour before the call of time. The full score was—Runcorn, two goals, three minors ; Lancashire, three minors. The teams were as follows :—Ruacorn : Full back,Houghton; three-quarters, Davies: Crompton, and Cawley; half-backs. 11. Hughes and Evans; forwards, Faulkner, W. Hughes, Hancock, Dolan, Gayter, J. Davies, Hampson, Rigby, and P. Riley. Lancashire : Back, T. Coop; three-quarters, J. Valen- tine, Barrett (Salford), and Winterbottom (Mossley) ; half backs, Marsden and Walsh (Salford) ; forwards, T. Kent (Salford), C. Horley, N. Hotchkiss' A. Paul, F. Bothwell, J. Sharpies, J. Hallam (all of Swinton), J. McGowan (Broughton Rangers), and H. Haselem. Amongst the visiting team were seven Lancashire county players.

div.head: FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES.
div.p: FOOTBALL MATCH AT WIDNES.

In aid of St'.-11.4;:i3;s7YjiTt-ig—Men's Society, Brass Band, a football match was played on the Widnes ground, on Thursday evening between 15 men of the Alkali Works, and 15 selected from the other works in the town. The latter team won easily by 2 goals (one dropped), 2 tries, 3 miners, to nil. Brennan dropped a goal and scored a try, and tries were also scored by Lally and Hardman. There were numerous spectators. BUILDING OPF:RATIONS AT RUNCORN. The Runcorn Commissioners at their meeting on Thurs- day approved the following plans :—Mr. James Ditch- field for the erection of a dwelling-house in Greenway- road ; Mr. James Kirkham for the erection of six cottages in Byron-st. ; Mr. John Waterworth for the erection of seven houses in Greenway-road and two houses in York- at.; Mr. Isaac Stubs for the erection of a seven stall stable at the Mineral Water Manufactory situate in Lowlands-road ; the Runcorn Property Company three houses in York-st.

BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN. The Foreign Missionary interim meeting was held on Sunday. Mr. Edward Taylor, one of the superinten- dents, occupied the chair, and Mr. Alfred Norman read a very encouraging report, the total receipts for the half year being £2B 19s. sd. The Rev. .T. Judson and Mr. B. Crosby were the speakers. Mr. Crosby gave a most interesting address on the missi n work in India, showing with what enormous difficulties our mission- aries had to contend, and referring especially to caste and the transmigration of souls. But notwith- standing all this there was much to thank God for and take courage. SPRING FAsHross, Spring Fashions.—J. & W. 1) =row, 16 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: YOUNG THIEF AT WIDNES.
div.p: A YOUNG THIEF AT WIDNES.

_ At Widnes Police Court., on Monday, Mary Ann Kinch- ley, 11 years of age, of Marsh-street, was charged with stealing 6d. from the person of Sarah Richards,: a girl, seven years of age. From the statement of Inspector Keighley it appear,d that a woman named Mrs. Critch- ley gave Richards 6d. to carry to Mr. Dodd's, draper, Waterloo-road. On the way she met the prisoner, who asked her if she might wrap the sixpence in paper. Richards consented, and on arriving at the shop she found that a halfpenny bad been substituted for the six- pence. The prisoner pleaded guilty and was fined 2s. fid. Mr. Deacon informed her that she would be sent to a reformatory if she offended again.

div.head: SUDDEN_DEATII AT WIDNES.
div.p: SUDDEN_DEATII AT WIDNES.

Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest at the West Bank Hotel, Widnes, on Tuesday, on the body of John Davieg, who lodged at 76, Church-st. It appeared that,since Christmas,Ditvies hod complained of pains near his heart and he had been under the treat- ment of Dr. McDonnell. On Saturday morning he went to his work apparently in his usual health and returned home in the evening at half-past eight. After washing and dressing himself, he went out and was afterwards seen both at the West Bank Hotel and the Bridge Hotel. He was assisted home from the latter place, falling twice on the way and he was placed on the sofa where he fell asleep. Next morning he was found to he dead and his neck and face were much discoloured.—A verdict of natural causes was returned. IRON BEDSTEADS & BEDDING.—Garland, 51, Bridge-st., Warrington. UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN • •

'ir.;;;; Humphreys, tke hon. sec, to the Oxford University Extension movement in Runcorn, has just received the report of the examiner (Mr. H. W. Bates, F.R.S., Royal Geographical Society), on the examination of students held on April 9tn. The examiner states that " the majority of the physiography papers from Runcorn are very fair performances, and give evidence that the writers have a sound knowledge of some of the chief physical laws involved in the questions answered. If none have reached a high proportion of marks, it is becausethe answers though accurate as far as they go, are not complete ; but this is a defect which will be re- paired by continuance of study ou the same lines as those hitherto followed." The resalt was as follows : Passed with distinction, Ist and prize, Henry H. Callis- ter ; 2nd, Margaret C. Callister ; 3rd, Sarah Comerford; 4th, William Epps; sth, Daniel S. Garner; 6th, Mary E. Joynson. Satisfied the examiner: Ist, Arthur Abram ; 2nd, Joseph M. Baguley ; 3rd, William Leathwood ; 4th, Thomas H. Parker ; sth, John Shingler. All the students who were examined have passed, a result that must be considered highly satisfactory.

GOSPEL MISSION HALL, RUNCORN. The first anniversary sermons were preached in the Hall en Sunday, by Mr. W. P. Roberts, of Liverpool. There were good congregations at each service. The choir sang appropriate musical pieces. The collections amounted to £l7 3s. 6d. On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the Hall, and there was a good attendancq. In the absence of Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., who was unable to be present, but forwarded a donation of two guineas, Mr. C. Garnett, occupied the chair and delivered an address.—Mr. Geo. Marshall, the leader of ,the Mission, read a financial statement, which showed that the Hall was built and furnished at a cost of £846; the builders contract being £725 10s. Towards the cost £l7B 18s 10d. was contributed in subscriptions, and various other small sums were obtained in various ways. Mr. Marshall had contribbted in a most generous manner out of his private purse and there was conse- quently only a debt of £3OO on the Hall. The accounts for the school and society were of a very satisfactory character. In the course of the proceedings stirring addresses were delivered by the Rev. C. Finch (Primitive Methodist), and the Rev. G. Thompson (Methodist Free Church.) The usual votes of thanks were passed.

BASE ROBBERY FROM A GIRL AT DITTON. Mary Jane Jackson, of Ditton, was brought before the Widnes magistrates on Monday, charged with having stolen half-a-sovereign from Mary Elizabeth Drought, a girl 11 years of age, who resides in Johnson-St., Ditton. On Saturday afternoon Mrs. Drought handed her daughter a purse, containing half-a-sovereign and several pawn tickets, axd instructed her to redeem several articles As the girl was walking towards the railway station she met the defendant, who asked her to bring a bundle from the pawnshop for her, and she went into her house. The prisoner asked her to fetch a gill of beer in order to get half-a-crown changed, and told her to leave her purse on the table as she might drop it on the way. She did so, and on returning she saw the prisoner place is. qd. and a pawn ticket in the purse. She did not open the purse until she got to the pawnshop, when she found that the half-sovereign had gone. She afterwards returned to Ditton, and told the prisonershe had lost her mother'shalf-sovereign, and pald the prisoner her money. In the course of the afternoon the prisoner made a pur- chase at the shop of Mr. James Evans, grocer, Ditton, and tendered half-a-sovereign in payment. She received 9s. odd in change. The prisoner was fined £l, or 14 days' hard labour. MARRIAGE OF MISS TAYLOR, OF RUNCORN. . •

A marriage in which more than ordinary interest was manifested was solemnized at Halton-road Wesleyan Chapel on Wednesday afternoon. The bride was Miss Lizzie Taylor, eldest daughter of Mr. Samuel Taylor, of Rydal Mount, Flalton-road, and the bridegroom was Mr. J. Mason Frith, second son of Mr. J. B. Frith, of Halton- road. Both the contracting parties are members of well- known and highly respected families in the town, and the happy event drew together a congregation that almost filled the spacious edifice, while hundreds re- mained outside to witness the arrival of tits guests, &c. There was a gay display of bunting in the neighbour- hood of the chapel and of the residences of the bride and bridegroom and flags fluttered in the breeze from many prominent points in the town. Near Rydal Mount a triumphant arch was erected. Before the arrival of the bridal party Mr. Fred Pope played appropriate selections of music. The bride who was attiled in a costume of electric blue cashmere, and wore a hat trimmed with pink roses, was led to the altar by her father. In attendance were two bridesmaids, Miss Janet Taylor and Miss Clara Taylor (sisters of the bride), and these ladies wore fawn-coloured dresses trimmed with brown velvet. The bride and bridesmaids carried bouquets of lovely flowers. The groomsmen were Mr. W. B. Frith and Mr. G. S. Frith (brothers of the bride- groom). The Rev. W. Kendrew conducted the service, which commenced with the wedding hymn "The voice that breathed o'er Eden:" At the conclusion of the cere- mony, and after the usual formula had been gone through in the vestry, the organ pealed forth the " Wedding March," and on emerging from the chapel, the happy couple were greeted with showers of rice, a performance that was repeated on arrival at Mr. Taylor's residence. A numerous wedding party sat down to lunch, and sub- sequently Mr. and Mrs. J. Mason Firth departed for Lon- don, en route for the Isle of Wight, where they intend to spend the honeymoon. The happy couple were the reci- pients of about a hundred handsome and valuable pre- sents, amongst which was a walnut workcase, given by the children attending Mill Brow Sunday School '; and a case of cutlery presented by the employes of the Runcorn Gasworks, of which Mr. J. R. Firth is the manager. The carriages were supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Bros., of Runcorn. On Thursday evening Mr. Frith gave the workmen of the Gas Company a capital supper at Mr. Riley's Coffee Tavern, Bridge-st., and the usual congrw- tulatory toasts were proposed and responded to.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The Lancashire County Council, on Thursday, discussed at considerable length the scheme for transferring the four county lunatic asylums to an asylums board, and finally resolve that the scheme formed a basis for dealing with the asylums ; that questions as to contributions and other matters of detail be referred to the committee; and that the Financial Adjustment Committee be requested to confer with the Lunatic Asylums Committee on such details. It was resolved to indict the St. Anne's-on-the-Sea Local Board of Health at the next assizes for declining so comely with an order from , the County Council to maintain and repair certain highways within their jurisdiction. div.head: RAILWAYS AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE RAILWAYS AND THE SHIP CANAL.

The Cheshire Lines Committee's Bill was, on Thursday,befors a Select Committee of the House of Lords. It purposes the construction of several small lines connecting the Ship Canal Docks at INlanchester with the main lines of the Committee's system. The learned Counsel for the promoters pointed out that the opening of the canal would, in all probability, develop an enormous traffic, and that the railway companies felt bound to make arrangements for the distribution of the traffic in the same way as they had already done at Liver- pool. The land proposed to betaken was at present uncovered, and was in the market for building pur- poses. The objection taken by the landowners was to any of the land being used for sidings, but the promoters held that, without ample siding accom- modadion. the running line would be of very little service. The petitioners were Lord Egerton of Tatton, Sir H. de Trafford, and Mr. Gratix.

CIIESHIRIt 'LINES RAILWAY. The fifteenth annual meeting of the Cheshire Lines Platelayers' and Workmen:4' Provident Society. which consists of the workmen employed in the engineers' department of the Cheshire Lines Rail- way, was held at the works, Battersby-lane. War- rington. on Wednesday evening, ,Mr. W. Corker, District Permanent IVay .Inspector, presided, and the meeting was largely attended by officials and delegates from Lancashire and Cheshire. The Secre- tary submitted the annual report, which stated that the number of members was 986. A large amount had been expended in aid of the 222, sick members who have received assistance from the funds of the society. and 17 death claims had also been paid. The report and statement of accounts having been passed, Mr. Thomas Pratt was re-elected secretary for the ensuing year, and the auditors, Messrs. D. S. Duncan and S. Dale were re-elected. The proceedings ter- minated with votes of thanks to the chairman, offi- cers, &c. TRAVELLIIC} TRUNICS.—Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge- et.. Warrington.
A ST. HELENS IRISHMAN AND THE ROYAL IRISH_CONSTADOLARY._

--- At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday. before Messrs. A. Sinclair, B. Birana and D. Mcliechnie, twe respectably dressed Irishmen named Michael O'Connor and James Daley, residents of Greenough- st., were charged with drunkenness. Evidence was given by P.C. Littler and another officer, who were cross-examined at some length by the defendants. O'Connor ultimately declared that the constable Littler would make a good memb-T of the R. I. C., adding that if the Chief Secretary for Ireland knew such a man as he was knocking about St. Helens, he would not be long before he was in Ireland. It was a confounded fraud to allow a man to swear like Littler had done. If Balfour knew about Littler he would soon have him over in the new Tipperary town swearing men's lives away there.—The Bench asked him to confine his observations to the case before them, and O'Connor replied: Why cannot I get fair justice when I come here? I am not guilty of the crime, and sure there's no use in com- ing here to look for justice.—Tbe Bench fined Daley 2s. 6d. and costs, and O'Connor ss, and Costs. div.head: ALLEGED PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ALLEGED PERMITTING DRUNKENNESS AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele, Wm. Joynson, keeper of the Shamrock Tavern,was summoned for having, on the 19th April, unlawfully permitted drunken- ness to take place on his premises. Inspector Bowyer stated that about 935 on Saturday night, the 19th April. he visited the Shamrock Tavern, in company with P. S. Gosling. In the taproom, be- hind the door, they saw Frederick Waller, who was drunk and had a pint cup half filled with beer before him. The 'landlady said she had not served him, and she went out and called in a young man from another room, who, after 'looking around as though he did not know what he was to do, olaimed the beer before Waller as his. There was a half pint porter bottle on the bar, and Waller said he had his in that. There was a great noise of music and singing upstairs, and the landlord came down and ordered Waller out. About half past eight he (witness) found a man named Seymour in Regent-st. with a broken leg and he bandaged the limb and conveyed the injured man to Dr. McDougall's surgery. Wailer followed them into the• surgery, and his conduct was such that Di. McDougall had to order him out. Waller was then drunk.—Dr. McDougall deposed that Waller was under the influence of drink at half-past eight. At '2O minutes to ten the landlord of the Shamrock Tavern brought Waller to the surgery, and asked him to examine him. He refused. Willer was then considerably worse than he was at half-past eight.—P.S. Gosling corroborated Inspector ' Bowyer's evidence.—Mr. Burton, Who appeared for the thffence, called Dr. Manran, who said Waller went to his surgery at half-past ten, and he *made an examin- ation of him. He could talk quite rationally, and he was quiet steady in his gait. The man had had some think but was not drunk, and he was quiet capable of taking care of himself.—Mrs. Sovrison, wife of. the defendant, said Waller left he house with Sey- I rnour at half-past seven, and she did not know he , was in the house when the officers called. The pint et beer belonged to Alfred Haddock, and she had , not served Waller with beer or a bottle of porter. Waller was able to walk straight and to talk properly. He was not drunk. The defendant was called, and said he was attending to the singing room upstairs, and he never saw Waller from the tim- of the disturbance in' the house when Waller left with Seymour, until the officers came in. He ordered Waller out, but found that he was not drunk,and took him to the police station, but the Superintendent was not in. He then went to Dr. McDougall's, hut the doctor refused to examine him,and eventually he was examined by Dr. Mangan. John Tar- bock, a bricklayer, said the disturbance was about a game of "Tip-it," which was a game they played for etas:4,s of beer. They were not playing then for beer. Wader went out after the disturbance, and he was not drunk. He had not been returned long when the police came and he had not been served. The beer in front of him be'onged to Dick Haddock. Peter Cawley, a water- man, also stated Waller was not drunk, and Waller was called and said all the drink he had was a pint of ale and a bottle of porter and he was not drunk. He was not supplied with anything after the "disturbance. Mr. Burton having addressed the bench for the defence, Mr. 'Thomas said the magistrates were of opinion Waller was drunk, but there was a doubt about pen:flitting drunken- ness and they gave Toynson the benefit of it and dis- missed the summons. Waller was then charged with being ,drunk, and was fined ss. and costs, 13s. 6d.

RLINCuRN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. The monthly meeting was held on Thursday, Mr. J. W. Lightburn presided, and there were present, Messrs. J. Pritchard, W. Fisher, F. Wiswall, S. Taylor, R. Morris, E. Timmins, E. Imison, W. Hankinson, H. J. Once, W. R. Wass, and W. Whit- taker ; P. A. Linaker (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), M. Barker (surveyor), Dr. McDougall (medical officer.) HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer of Health reported that the number of deaths registered during April amounted to 32, of these one was an inquest case and of the remaining deaths eight were due to mesenteric disease, two to apoplexy, three to premature birth, three to inflam- mation of the bowels, two each to convulsions, pthisis, natural decay, pneumonia, bronchitis, and one each to inflammation of stomach, disease of brain, intestinal obstruction, chronic kidney disease,and pleurisy follow- ing child-birth. The 32 deaths showed an average death- rate of 21.3 per 1,000 per annum of the estimated population. THE NEW ROAD.
The Highways and Building Committee made the following recommendations with regard to the proposed

new toad from Heath-road to Greenway-road : That the offer of the Manchester Ship Canal Company as contained in their letter of November 19th, 1889, to make an embankment and viaduct in such part ot the proposed new road its would traverse the property of the said company, be accepted. That the offer of Major J. C. Orred as contained in the letter of his agent, Mr. C. L, i Evans, of the N)th January, 1890, and n subsequent correspondence, to give land and the sum of £l,OOO, less the cost of fencing for the making of the said road, as settled at. an interview between Mr. Evans and the committee, on the 31st March, be accepted. —The above-named recommendations are subject to agreements being entered into between the respective parties. It was further recommended that this Board contribute the sum of £l,lOO towards' the expenses of making the said road.—Mr. Taylor moved the adoption of the minutes, and said a road from Heath-road to Greenwav-road would be a great advantage to the rate- payers of Runcorn; and the offer of the Ship Canal was to construct a viaduct, and was a very liberal one. Major Orred offered to give land and £l,OOO towards making a road fromthe viaduct to the extent of his land By means of thve two offers, the ratepayers could, at little cost, make a most excellent road, 36 feet wide which would ease the traffic through the town consider- ably and avoid the declivity from Delphs Bridge to the Police Station and then the incline from the latter place to the railway station. The new road would provide a much nearer way from both Halton-rd. and Heath-rd., to Runcorn Station, Higher Runcorn, and Weston, and he was sure would be a very great boon to the town.— Mr. Grice seconded the motion and expressed his !?rati- fication that the Board had come to the conclusion to accept the offers. It must be evident to all the ratepay- ers that the proposed road was a step in the right direc- tion, and would be of great advantage in the future development of the town.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: WORK IN COMMITTEE.
div.p: WORK IN COMMITTEE.

The Finance Committee reported that during the month the receipts amounted to £52 18s. 11d, and accounts amounting to £351 3s. 3d. on general fund, and £lOO on loan account were passed for payment.—The Library Committee reported that owing to the inconvenience of the present entrance to the Free Library and also the overcrowding which takes place on these nights when the School Board have occasion to bring negligent parents before them, it is desirable that a new approach to the Library and reading rooms be made from Waterloo-road to the side door facing the lawn, and the Committee recommend that such new approach be made.—This minute was referred to the Finance Committee.

WATERLOO BRIDGE. The Committee recommended that the work in con- nection with the stone pillars and ironwork of Waterloo Bridge be proceeded with in accordance with the modi- fied plans prepared by Mr. Walter Timmins, and that tenders be invited for the execution of the work.—Mr. Pritchard proposed the adoption of the minutes, and said the plans had been carefully considered by the Commit- teP and they had dispensed with everything they could of a costly nature. but a considerable amount of iron- work would be required, and in fact this was the most costly part of the work.—The minute was approved.

NIGHTSOIL REMOVAL. On the recommendation of a special Committee, it was resolved to purchase for the purpose of nightsoil removal, two horses from Mr. Field for £5O, also a cart, two sets of harness, &c. It was further resolved to engage one foreman carter at a rate not exceeding 265. 6d. per week, and another carter at the rate of 245. per week, and men for the emptying of ashpits at a rate not exceeding 453. per working night; also a boatman at wages not exceed- ing 303. per week. In the event of being necessary it was decided to hire a boat from Mr. Field at £1 per week. The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Pritchard.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. H. Wade Deacon and Mr. J. Brock. .

DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence a fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Michael Malone. model lodging-house; T. Handley, Appleton; Martin Walsh, 5, Cromwell-st.; Francis Tansey, Victoria-st. ; and Rebecca Airlie, no residence. Jas. Brown, 21, Elizabeth-St.; was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly, and 103. and costs for assaulting P.C. Wolfenden while in the execu- tion of his duty.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TllollBDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brock, and Lieutenant Col.

Gaskell. Wrivnow SMASHING.—For smashing the windows of the house of Samuel Eyes, of Major Cross-st., Mary Swift, of no fixed residence, was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs and the damage, in all 195., or go to gaol for seven days. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—John Bentham, Chohnon- deley-st., and Patrick Morgan, no residence, were each fined 55., and Michael Redmond, Marsh-st., was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. John Rogers, Pool-st., and Agnes Mulroy, Catherine-st., were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, for creating breaches of the peace. DOG AT LARGE.—Edward Lloyd. Mersey-road, was fined 2s. 6d. add costs for allowing his dog to be at large, unmuzzled. COMPULSORY EDUCATION.—The School Board sum- moned a number of persons for not sending their chil- dren regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. IN PURSUIT OF GAME—William Dunn, of Victoria-st., was summoned for having on the 27th ult. at Cronton, trespassed on the land of Mr. Frederick Wm. Young in pursuit of game. Evidence was given to the effect that the defendant was in a wood on the estate beating about as though in search of game.—Mr. Knowles, who de- fended, said the fact of the defendant being in the wood did not prove that he was poaching, but the Bench thought he was searching for game, but it was not a bad case, and as it was his first offence, they would not record a conviction. He would have to pay costs.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele. DOGS AT LAW:Gt.—George Turley. Norton Arms, Hal- ton, was fined 6d. and costs for allowing his dog to be large unmuzzled.—For a like offence, in Trinity-street, Thomas Heath Barton was fined Bd. and costs, 8s fid. Scnoot. BOARD CASES.—Ii number of parents were summoned by the School Board for not sending their children regtilarly to school, and the usual fine of 8d and costs, 4s ed, was inmoaed in each case. CHGANNY ON Ftsul.—Peter Bradbury, of Regent-street, was fined 6d and costs for allowing the chimney of his dwelling to bison fire. DEIGN! AND DISORDBRLY.—For this offence H. Peter Bradbury was fined ss. and costs, 9s. 6d., and Sarah Ann Dunban was fined 2s. 6d. and costs, Bs. 10d. Reataisogn.—Thomas Davy, a young man, was again remanded on a charge of having stolen a quantity of wearing apparel from the schooner Bessie, the property of Henry Forster and Thomas Quirke.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

FATAL ALCCTDENT AT Kiwosunr.--Ori Friday morning week, a shocking accident befell Mr. W. E. Gibson, of the Water Mill, Kingsley. It would appear that, whilst the deoeased was in the act of jumping off some sacks of meal in Hs mill, he fell on to the handle of a hand-truck which after tearing his trousers inflicted serious irgaries, from the effects of which he died on Monday, in spite of the mecEcal aid rendered by Dr. Smith of Weaverilam. On Tuesday an inquest was held by Mr. C. W. Tlbbits (deputy coroner) at the residence of the deceased at which a 'verdict of "Death by accident" was sebarned. Mr. Gibson was a well-known and much respected man. fie leaves a widow and four children.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.
8A.T.1. AT SANKR;
Last idight a ball wasTeld—a-t"-giiaey, the,eccasion being the breaking up of the Penketh Conservative Club dancing class for the season. MAY DAY. - - -

The Ist of May was celebrated in Penketh by a' prooession of chi,ldren headed by a carriageKcontain- sag the' May Queen." The weather was splendid and the appearance of the children was very pleas- ing and afforded great pleasure to those who wit-, nessed the parade. PENESZE FIELD CLCE. The first ramble of the newly-organised Field , Club in connection with the Peuketh Wesleyan' Mutual Improvement Association was taken on Sat urday. The afternoon was showery, and un-,' favourable for a long ramble, so it was determined ,to go through the fields round about Sankey. Eighteen members and friends ' started from the Wesleyan Sunday School o.t 2.30 p.m., going by way of Liogley Green, Ohl Barrow Hall, or Moat House. again crossing the fields which lead to Sankey Rail- way Station, then along by Greystone Heath back to the school, which was reached shortly after five o'clock. A number of interesting specimens were gathered. After a short rest, tea was partaken of. It bad been vrovided by Miss Garnett. About twenty sat down, and it was evident that the ramble had prepared most of them for what had to follow. Afterwards the room was re-arranged, and the speci- mens brought out. Messrs. J. Peers, John F. Hills, and Thomas Gandy explained the different species of plants, and an enjoyable evening was spent. It is proposed to hold these rambles monthly, and, under tile guidance of the above-mentioned gentle- men, the scheme is almost sure to be a success.

div.head: RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT LEICESTER.
div.p: RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT LEICESTER.

_ On Wednesday night a collision occurred at Leicester Station, on the Midland line. A.North-Western train from Nuneaton had just been cleared, and was being moved down the line, when a passenger train from Bed- ford ran in, and the driver failing to pull up at the Proper moment, the engine dashed into the brake van of the North-Western train, •which was damaged, and the next coach thrown off the line. The passengers were shaken, but none of them were hurt. The line was soon cleared.

THE BLACK SPOTS OF WARRINGTON. REPORT BY THE MEDICAL OFFICER. The annual report of Dr. Hornell, the Medical Officer for the borough, hes just been issued to members of the Town Council. In it Dr. Gorindl deals with the sanitary condition of the different wards of the town, and, as this part of the report bears upon a subject which has been referred to in these columns, we give copious extracts from it.

'THE NORTH-WEST WARD With regard to the North-West Ward, Dr. Gomall says, " the main streets as a rule are well paved and cleansed. Perhaps the most serious defects to be noticed in this Ward are those due ti the unmade state of the back pasaages. Over Bowsey Bridge, in the neighbourhood of Lilford-street, Pierpoint-street, Catherine-street, and Hoyle-atreet, at the time of my visit some of the passages were in such a condition as nearly to be impas- &tile, their construction being so defective, by being so much higher than the yards, as seriously to interfere with the removal of the pails. In many cases the pails were embedded in soil, so that in removing a full pail the contents would be spilt over ;in fact, in numerous cases, the pail stood in a small cesspool of solid and liquid ex- creta. The yards in this district, are, with very few ex- ceptions, unpaved, and are therefore not kept clean, a clean yard being quite a novelty. In many instances an open rain spout empties the rain water on to the yard surface, causing dampness of the walls and of the foun- dations of the houses. There is also a large number of fowls, &c. kept in this district, which gradually causes a poisoned condition of the soil of the yards and passages, and this, with the deposit of exeneta by children, andtlie tendency of householders to throw refuse on an unmade , surface, adds to the many dangers to health which exist in this district. The next block of property, where the above description will generally apply, is situated in the neighbourhood of Tanner's-lane, viz. :—Erwood-st. and Portland-st. These houses were originally of the worst description, and are most deficiently kept in repair. Though the streets are well made of setts, the back pas- sages and yards are as unsanitary as they possibly can he. The majority of the houses with no ventilation, in this Ward, are wructurally very defective; in the majo- rity of cases the surrounding land or surface of yard, or passage, is unpaved. NORTH-EAST WARD. This ward enjoys the unenviable privilege of having the highest death rate. It has the largest number of back- to-back houses, and houses with no through ventilation, and there are other dwellings where there are restrictions and impediments to the free circulation of air. This ward is also the most over-crowded, and, unfortunately, remarkable for "Domestic Darkness" and general dirti- ness of dwellings. Dr. Ballard describes this condition as "Fustiness." In my inspection I found it characteristic of the dwellings in Havdock-st., Silver-st., Tilley-st., &c., &c. The houses in Haydock-st are old and dilapidated and badly kept in repair, the walls are generally damp, the mortar between the bricks perished, the surface of yards most defective,pail closets imperfect, the grids of traps absent, slop water soaking into the surface of yard. The passages to the various courts had invariably that smell of fustiness due to the deposit ot excreta and other filth, and the difficul,y of cleansing an unmade and imperfect surface. Passing on to Silver-st. where many of the houses are back to back ,there is deficient closet accommodation, and the passage betweeß Silver- square and Olive-st . is in a most filthy state. Silver-square is still unmade; if properly excavated and paved with sets it might be ,nade sanitary arid a great c nnfort to the poor who live in this locality. In the Hardy-st. district the streets are unmade; of this you are already aware. The same defects as described in North-west Ward exist in the yards and back passages. In the Crossley-st. dis- trict the passages are in a terrible state. In Back Crossley-st., there was abundance of decomposing organic matter, which must, under favourable circum- stances, cause a pollution of the atmosphere and thus lower the standard of health. In the yards of Tilley-st. there is the usual want of ventilation. Eldon-st. is still unmade. William-st. and Back William-st. both contain property of a defective character. IR Manchester-road I there are several hack-to-back houses which could, with great ease, be made into through houses. Of this class of property, in this ward alone, there are nearly 300 so II calledliouses without through ventilation. SOUTH-EAST, LATCHFORD, AND SOUTH-WEST WARDS. The general sanitary condition of these wards, taken as a whole, is an improvement on the condition of the two North wards. In the twolatter there is much which tends torender them unhealthy, whilst in the other three wards, though the same remarks may be applied to the back passages, the unsanitary condition of the courts off Church-street, the unmade streets in the neighbourhood of Howley and Knutsford-rbad, the unhealthy dwellings in Dolman's-lane, Ship-yard, Old-road, Latchford, and Factory-lane, Bank Quay ; yet there are more breathing spaces, the thoroughfares are straighter, not so narrow, nor are the people so hemmed in by high buildings and business premises, preventing a free circulation of air. This is only a supertcial report, and is in accordance wirh the duties of the Medical Officer of Health " that he shall, by inspection of the district, both systematically, at certain periods, and at intervals as occasion may re- quire, keep himself informed of the conditions injurious to health." I add also a synopsis of Dr. Ballard's recom- mendations in his recent report on the causation of infantile diarrhea, which has considerable bearing on our present sanitary condition." In another part of his report, Dr. Gornall expresses the hope that during the year 1890, the attention of the Town Council will be directed to the serious evils arising from "the unhealthy areas" and "unsanitary dwell- ings" which still exist in the barough. This is a subject, he adds, which is occupying the minds of sanitarians all over the country, and he feels sure they would not allow. Warrington to take a secondary place.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The movement set on foot by Mr. James White, with the object of making a presentation to Superintendent Johnstone of Widnes, on his retire- ment from the force, will meet with general approval. Although Mr. Johnstone's stay amongst us has been brief, yet he is the first superintendent of Widnes, and by his unfailing courtesy and kind- ness, he has won golden opinions from all with whom he has been brought in contact, and he could not be allowed to depart without carrying with him some little memento from the Chemical Metro- polis. A. capital cemmittee of tradesmen and others has been formed to receive subscriptions, and there will without doubt be a generous response to their appeal. It is rumoured that Inspector Noblett, of Over Darwen, has been appointed Mr. Johnstone's suc- cessor, but no official notification to that effect has been received, and it is probable that the appoint- meat has not yet been filled. It appears from this month's Parish Magazine that the !bellringers of Runcorn Church are in a fair way to have their grievance settled. About the middle Of last year the ringers "struck work" on a dispute as to the mode of obtaining their wages, and a new set of ringers had to be obtained. The strikers claimed half a year's wages, but the Vicar's Warden csntended they were not engaged to ring and were not entitled to any payment. There was a feeling abroad that if the men were not legally entitled, they were morally, and others who hold that opinion have subscribed the Min of £5 to settle the matter. What a pity this was act done earlier- and various little unpleasantness prevented. There is &likelihood that what has been thought of and talked of for years—i.e. a road from Beath- road to ereenway-road, will, in a short time be an accomplished fact. It is very kind of the Ship Canal Company to build the necessary viaduct over the Big Pool, and of Major Orred to give the land for the road and a thousand pounds towards the expense of its construction, bat it must not be lost zihtof'that these two parties will benefit to a larger extent than anyone else from the construction of the road. At the same time the road will be a con- eiderable improvement to the town, and will be of even greater advantage as the years roll by, and the ratepayers are paying their full share when they contribute £l,lOO to the cost. The rate for the present year is an increa.se of 2d. on last year, and next year there will probably be a further increase, so that the raiepayers are likely to cry out that they are paying too dearly for improvements. At the adjourned vestry meeting at Runcorn, last week, the feet of Nonconformists being asked to retire frotn the church vestry was incidentally reviewed. On the one hand Mr. Coleburn questioned the Vices right to make such a request, as all ratepayers were parishioners; while on the other hand Mr. Imison and Mr. Mellor argued that it was not fair, and pointed out that Churcbpeople " magmiminously allowed Nonconformists to manage their own chapel affairs. There is but this differ- ence lathe two cases. The Nonconformist places of worship are built by the voluntary subscriptions of a sect, and Runcorn Parish Church was built by the proceeds of a compulsory rate, levied on all ratepayers, irrespective of creed or profession. Be- sides, the churchwardens and sidesmen are parish officers. and as such ought to render to the whole parish an account of bow they deal with the monies that come into their hands. "Outsiders" do not wish to interfere in the management of the Parish Church—they are waiting for disestablishment— but when it comes-to a question of right there is no doubt that all ratepayers have a perfect right to attend and take part in the Parish Church vestry.

MEETING OF CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The quarterly meeting of this Council-Vias held on Thursday at Chester Castle, when Mr. Duncan Graham, the chairman, presided over a large atten- dance. The Chairman announced that letters of apology for absence had baen received from the Duke of Westminster, Lord Egerton and other members. The Chairman laid before the Council the corres- pondence received from the Local Government , Board respecting an application made to them by the Lancashire County Council for the constitution of a joint committee representing several adminis- trative counties in the watershed of the riVers Irwell and Mersey. for the purpose of enforcing the Rivers Pollution Prevention Act, 1876. The Ches- hire Council's reply to the Board mentioned that the extension of the area as proposed by the Lanca- shire County Council did not seem to have any advantages,but had great disadvantages; and that there was no necessity for the enlarged district pro- posed by the Lancashire County Conncil. It was decided to forward the reply. A committee was appointed to consider and deal with questions arising regarding the formation of a joint Committee. The meetings of the County Council during the next twelve months will be held in Chester Town Hall Council-chamber. Dr. Atkinson moved the adoption of the Finance Committee's minutes, which showed that there was a balance on the county fund account at Slst March last of £55,532, whilst there was a credit balance at the bank on the 171 April of £27,914. After deducting liabilities to 31st March last there would be a balance to be carried to the credit' of the cur- rent year's budget amounting to .£24,757. Mr. J. J. Evans seconded, and the minutes were adopted. On the prolaosition of Dr. Atkinson, seconded by Colonel France-Hayhurst, the Council voted a superannuation allowance to Mr. Charles Townsend, of .£266, as compensation for the abolition of his office as county treasurer. Dr. Atkinson prewnted the buJget for the year 1890-1. It indicated an estimated expenditure of £187.738, and it was recommended that a -county rate of 14d. in the pound be levied for the purposes of the county for the ensuing six months; and that a general police rate of Id in the pound, together with ad litional local police rates, be also levied. Mr. J. J. Evans seconded the motion. Dr. Atkinson moved, Mr. C. Welch seconded, and it was carried, that the executive committee under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Acts be requested to provide for the payment of compensa- tion for cattle slaughtered, and that the Council place the sum of £l,OOO to a separate account to meet the payments. On the proposition of Mr. J. C. Antrobus, seconded by Alderman T. Beeley, the Council granted the sum of .£l,OOO, in addition to the £6,000 already granted, for improvements at Parkside Asylum. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION.

- Mr. T. Rigby called attention to the Technical Instruction Act, 1889, and moved for the appoint- ment of a committee to consider the desirability of the County Council supplying or aiding the supply of technical or manual instruction, and to report thereon to a subsequent meeting of the Council. Mr. C. E. Thorneycroft seconded the resolution, which was carried, and the following committee was appointed :—Lord Egerton, lion. W. P. Tolle- mache, Messrs. Thorneycroft, G. Dixon, J. F. Cheet- ham, G. Cooke, C. B. Davies, J. Edwards, R. Bate, J. Smale, T. Parker, T. Rigby, W. R. Harp, and Dr. Hewitt.
Other minor Motions having been passed, the Council postponed the remainder of the business to the next meeting in August.

div.head: CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.
div.p: CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL, WARRINGTON.

SALE OF WORK. Yesterday afternoon there was opened, by Miss Valentine, of Hale, in Cairo-st. schoolroom, a sale of home industries and exhibition of thrift work, under the auspices of the Ladies' Sewing Society. The object of the exhibition was "to encourage thrift and industry in the home by showing how otherwise useless things and idle hours may be turned to profitable and interesting results." The proceeds of the sale are to be devoted to the school extension fund for providing an increase of class- room accommodation. The exhibition Was denom- inated "The Thrifteries " on the catalogue, and the various sections were under the charge of the ladies and gentlemen named :-1. Loan exhibition, Mrs. Long, Mrs. Walker, Mrs. Monks, Mrs. Priestman; 2, home industries, Mrs. Winser, Mrs. Mullard, Miss Wheeler, Mrs. Tunstall, and Mrs. Briggs; 3, thrift and toy stall, Mrs. F. Freeston, Mrs. J. It. Young. Miss Long, Miss Monks; 4, book stall, Rev. F. K. Freeston; 5, flower stall, Miss G. Milner, Miss M. Monks, Miss E. Monks; 6, girls' stall, Miss Houghton and Miss Wor- rell ;7, home cookery, Miss Knowles; 8, wood carving, Mr. J. Monks and Mr. T. Kinnaird ; 9, refreshments, Miss Allen and Miss Knowles; 10, the thrift cottage, Mr. T. Knowles and Mr. G. Eden. On the different stalls there were many useful and ornamental articles, and numerous examples of ingenious handiwork. One of the most interesting parts of the exhibition was the " thrift cottage" designed by Mrs. W. Long to show how inex- pensively a cottage sitting-room and bedroom may be tastefully furnished. Among the furnishings of this model cottage were a bonnet box made out of a dis- carded tea chest, a neat little cradle the main part of which consisted of an old soap box, and an ornamental case for a small clock constructed out of a cigar case_ At the time of the opening there was a good attend- ance, including the Rev. F. K. and Mrs. Freeston the Rev. T. L. Jones (Liverpool), the Rev. J. C. ?Rust (Hale), Miss Valentine (Hale), Mr. and Mrs. W. Long, Mr. and Mrs. F. and the Misses Monks, Mr. and Mrs. F. W. Monks. Mr. and Mrs. J. Winser, Mr. T. Birchall, Mrs. J. Worthington (Sale), Mrs. Houghton (Knutsford), Mrs. and the Misses Broadbent, Mrs. Chorley, Mrs. Gibson Smith, Miss C. Harvey, Mrs. Freeston (Macclesfield), 8:c. The Rev. F. K. FREESTON said that the sewing society held there for some years had, he believed on the sug- gestion of Mrs. Long, determined to inaugurate a new departure in their method of work, in other words to work a new idea. They had, he supposed, all aither• attended or heard of the "Healtheries, "The Fisheries,'" "The Colinderies," and so forth, but he ventured to, think not many of them had had an opportunity of at- tending" The Thrifteries." The object of that bazaar was to encourage the idea of thrift and industry in the homes of their people by showing how useless things and idle hours might be turned to profitable results. On the other hand, the work of the school there had for some time been carried on under great disadvantages. The school had increased in numbers to nearly 300 and they had very little class-room accommodation. Their friend' Mr. Monks, had offered them a large donation, and with the object of increasing the fund the ladies of the Sewing Society very readily consented that the proceeds of their work should be devoted to increasing thc class-room accommodation. They had, therefore, two objects before them—to encourage thrift and to help the funds for the enlargement of the Sunday school. (Hear. hear.) Mks VALENTINE then opened the sale of work. She remarked that that work was very interesting to her, and, indeed, in a small way, she had some of it on her own hands. She congratulated those who had done the work and upon the SUM'S.% that had attended their efforts. (Applause.) Councillor MONKS moved a vote of thanks to Miss Valentine. Mr. T. HIRCIIALL seconded the proposal, which was cordially adopted, and Mr. W. Long responded on behalf of Migs Valentine. The Rev. F. K. Freston then announoed that the fol- lowing contributions had been received :—Mr. W. 1). Houghton, £lO ; Mr.W.Robson, :22 ; and Miss Valentine,, £lO.

The sale was then proceeded with. It will be con- tintiebto-day (Saturday). The proceedings of yesterday's sale amounted to £7l. The Queen has approved the nomination of the Rey.. Daniel Lewis Lloyd, head masner of Christ's College, Brecon, to the bishopric of Bangor, in the room of the Right Rey. James Colquhoun Campbell. resigned. During the hearing of a charge of stealing a silk hand- kerchief against William Brown, aged 24. at the Thames. Police Court, on Tuesday, it transpired that the accused- had been married eleven' years, aid that he became a father in his fourteenth year. He Was released on a surety coming forward on his behalf. THE TRIPLE BIRTH. The Rev. 11. S. Bolton, vicar of Ravenhead, has suc— ceeded in procuring the Queen's bounty for Evan Edwards, whose wife last month gave birth tn three girls. The Vicar represented the circumstances of the family to her Majesty, and has received £3 through Sir Henry Ponsonby. the children were named Margaret Arnold, Elizabeth Anne, and Ellen, but the latter has since died.

A SCENE AT WARRINGTON BRIDGE. Early on Sunday afternoon, as a cab containing Dr. Sherratt was being driven over Warrington bridge, a waggonette came up from the opposite direction as the corner into Wilderspool-road was being rounded. At the same moment Dr. Starkey Smith's hansom, coming from Latchford, drove up. The driver of the cab was unable to check his horse, but avoided a collision. It was, however, done at the expense of some damage to the Cheshire Supply Stores, as the shaft§ of the cab penetrated the shutters and smashed a plate glasswindow. Neither the driver nor the horse was injured.

div.head: PARALLEL LINES.
div.p: PARALLEL LINES.

EVERY student knows that in close reasoning parallel lines of thought are laid down and deductions educed. It is not ouz purpose at this time to enterinto a learned ' discussion, and we have drawn the above visible lines simply to bring them prominently before your eye; and to ask what they represent to you. A railroad man to whom we showed them, said, " To me those four lines represent a double-track railway." A doctor replied to the same interrogatory, "The lines are to me the large arteries and veins lying along- side each other in the human body." As will be observed, the same lines to either gentle- man suggested different lines of thought, as both looked at them through eyes ie,customed to see only that which for the most part occupied their attentipn. To the writer, both answers put an old truth in a fresh and °original light. As every intelligent man or woman knows, the blood of every living person flows with almost railway speed through the arteries, forced by that wonderful engine, the heart. From the arteries it is side-tracked through the capillaries and veins, and every drop of blood goes ;through the kidney for purification no less than 2,500 times every twenty-four hours. If the kidneys be diseased, the impurities of the blood containing the worn- out tissues and deleterious acids are not drawn out or excreted as Nature intended, but continually pass and repass through every fibre of the system, carrying death and decay with every pulsation. Unless remedied the , heart becomes weakened, the lungs trying to do double work break down, the liver becomes congested, the stomach refuses to digest food, and the result is a general break down. Why? Because the kidneys, the sewers of the system, are foul and stopped up, and the entire blood becomes nothing more nor less than sewerage. Now, is it not criminal, nay, suicidal, to allow such a state of things to continue when a simple remedy is with- in your reach, knows for a certainty to do as repre- sented, which will t..pen the closed pipes of the kidneys, allow the effete matter to escape, relieve the overworked heart, lungs, and liver, cause a healthy appetite, put the bloom of health in your cheek, the dove of hope in your breast, and the light of life in your eye ? You already have divined the remedy we have refer- ence to ; its praise is universal, its influence world-wide. Do not allow prejudice to blind you to your best inter- ests. but to-day procure Warner's' SAFE" Cure, which can be procured of all chemists, at 4s. ed. and 2s. 9s. per bottle, and be put on the straight road to rugged health and correct living. Our parallel and closing lines to you are, take our advice and your experience will justify you in thanking us for bringing under your notice a remedy without parallel.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
A Cußtors CASE.

A respectably-dressedna--n;t7ed Frederick Rushton was brought before the Warrington magistrates, on Tuesday morning, under peculiar circumstance. On the night previous Constable Turner was called to the Co-operative Stores, where he found. Rushton lying on a form. In answer to a query. Rushton said that he had "gone there for the handicap," and the constable, think- ing that his mind was wandering, locked him up for safety. He now gave an intelligible account of himself, and was discharged. A TIPSV DEFENDANT CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING HIS WIFE.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, an elderly an named Isaac Smith was summoned for haying assaulted his wife. Complainant described the assault, and said that for some time she had been sub- jected to ill usage at the hands of her husband. Defend- aqt, who was tipsy, attempted to address the Bench, but he was put back until this (Saturday) morning, it being palpable that be was not fit to plead.
HOW PITCH AND Toss PLAYERS COMBINE.

A young man named John Thos. Forsyth was charged at the Warrington Borough Court on Monday with hav- ing played at pitch and toss in Birchall-st. He denied the allegation, and said he was a quite innocent onlooker and did not know the name of even one of the players. The magistrates, however, accepted the police-con- stable's version of the affair, and imposed a fine of ss. and costs. The Chief Constable said those who were caught playing pitch and toss never under any circum- stances knew the names of the other players, but aftet a fine was inflicted a subscription was made all round to meet the expenses of the party who was fined. A STREET PRST. John Garrity, a young man who had been before the Bench several times before,was sentenced to two months' ' hard labour at the Warrington Borough Court, on Mon- day, for a very unprovoked assault on Thomas Rowlands, a cab driver, and his wife. Mr. and Mrs. Rowlands were coming up Bridge-st. rather late at night when Garrity asked Rowlands for a penny for a "doss." and because he didn't get it he struck Rowlands. When Mrs. Row- lands expostulated he hit her too. The Chief Constable said the offence was very characteristic of the prisoner, as he was always assaulting people in this way. The sentence mentioned above was then passed upon Garrity.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATuanAr.—Before Alderman Burgess, Councillor Voisey,
and Mr. B. Gaett
DarrmtENNEss.—For having been diunk and disorderly on Town Hill on the previous night, Patrick Waldren was fined ss. and costs. MONDAT.—Bcfore the Mayor (Alderman Francomb),
Alderman Davies, and Alderman Harrison.

DRUNICE.NNESS.—Bridget McDonough, drunk and dis- orderly at Market-gate, on Saturday night, fined lock-up fees 25.; Thomas Barrett, drunk and disorderly, Butter- market-st., Saturday night, fined 2s. ed. ; Anne Richard- son, drunk and disorderly, Wilderspool-road, Saturday night, fined ss. ; Alice Thomas, drunk and disorderly, Buttermarket-st. Whalley, for being asleep whilst in charge of two horses and a lurry, at Appleton, on the 4th April. fined is. and costs; Michael Moore, for driving a cart and horse without reins, at Lower Walton, on the 18th April, was ordered to pay costs. THE Rent's HEAD, GRAPPENHALL. ^ Alfred Chaplin, landlord of the Ram's Head Inn, Grappenhall, was charged with having unlawfully kept his house open at a time it should have been closed on Easter Sunday; and Wm. Raymond, also of Grappenhall, was charged with having been on the licensed premises. From the evi- dence of P.C.'s Millington and Bennett, it appeared that about a quarter-past ten o'clock on Easter Sunday morn- ing they found two men named John Smith and Wm. Smith in a shed at the back of the Ram's Head. The landlord directly after brought in some beer in a half- gallon can, and on being questioned by the officers, he , said that John Smith was a workman of his, and Wm. Smith had come from Hollins Green. Chaplin also called in Raymond, who had been down the garden, and gave him some drink.—Mr. A. Browne, who de- fended, said his client asserted that he had been perse- cuted for a long time by Constable Millington, and his business had been practically ruined by that officer. It was also stated that Millington had recently said to Chaplin, "Thou has done me once, but if I cannot do thee one way, I'll do thee another," and the words of the officer had been written down in a book at the time by a man named William Wheeler, who was in the Ram's Head when they were used.—Evidence having been given for the defence, the magistrates said that although the case was not without an element of suspicion, there was not sufficient evidence to convict upon. The case was therefore dismissed.

THE CONTAGIOUS DISEASES (ANIMALS) ACT.—Peter Hall was charged with having, on :the 31st March, at Acton Grange, acted in contravention of an order made under the Contagious Diseases (Animals) Act by not isolating a certain cow which he had purchased from Mr. William Bennett, at Padgate, and was fined ss. and Costs. CRUELTY TO a HORSE.—William Nuttall was charged with cruelly ill-treating a horse on the canal bank at Moore, on the Ist April, by working it while in an unfit condition. Defendant said he was poor, and was obliged to work the horse. He denied, however, that it was in a poor condition.—Defendant was fined 10s. and costs, Mr. Parr remarking that this was a case of gross cruelty. _ . .
