ALLEGED THEFT AT WHITLEY.—ThrPe young tnen, Jas. Cliffe, William Cliffe. and Joseph Cliffe, were charged with stealing two sacks of oats and two empty sacks, the property of Mr. Alfred Barber, at Whitley Superior, on the 18th April.—The prisoners were represented by Mr. A. Browne.—The prosecutor said he was a farmer, and lived at Whitley Superior. At 3 p.m. on the 16th April he, in company with his wife, counted some sacks of black oats in the root-house of his buildings. At that time there were eight sacks He then went to Warring- ton, and on his return, from something that was said to him, he went to the root-house and counted the sacks of oats, and found only seven. He gave information to the police. He, in company with P.C. Bratt, searched the stable of the prisoner James Cliffe. The two sacks of black oats produced, and also the • two empty sacks produced, were found, which ho could identify as his property by the letters " J.T.G.F." P.C. Bratt removed the bags to prosecutor's house.—Mrs. Barber deposed to seeing Joseph Cliffe go into her husband's 11 root-house and stay there some time.—Constable Bratt, stationed at Stretton, said he w • to James Cliffe's

stable, where he found the tvr) saciss of oats produced. They were covered by a horse cloth. He also found two empty sacks, and Mr. Barber identified them all as his property.—Witness took possession of the oats and sacks, and went to James Cliffe's house in comi4any with Mr. Barber and knocked him up. He cams downstairs, got through the back window, and escaped for a time, but he was afterwards taken in charge for stealing two sacks of oats and two empty sacks, and he replied "Very well." Be was taken to Stockton Heath, and locked up, when he said " Bratt,l am very sorry for what I've done, but don't make it any blacker against me than you can help." On the next day he heard James Cliffe say "Master, you don't know that Joe and Bill is every bit as bad as me, but they are old servants, but don't bring them into it."—The Bench decided there was no case againstkWilliam and Joseph Cliff°, who were accordingly discharged.—ln the case of Jams Cliffe, the Bench thought the case against the prisoner had been proved, and fined him LS and costs.

div.head: BRIXTON MURDER.
div.p: THE BRIXTON MURDER.

The man Gorrie, charged with wilfully murdering Thomas Furlonger at Nevin's Bakery, Brixton, was on Tuesday formally committed for trial at the Central Criminal Court. Be reserves his defence. Further police evidence was given, and two doctors described the wounds on deceased's head, and the result generally of the post-mortem. Some small bloodstains had been found on some of the prisoner's garments.

Mr. Inskip, the Unionist candidate for East Bristol, has issued an address. He says the great question which divided the community at thelast general election retains all its practical importance, and he claims support as a defender of an undivided Empire, which has been bene- ficial to Ireland as well as to England and Scotland. Sir Joseph Weston, the Gladstonian candidate, has declared in favour of an eight hours' bill for miners and dangerous occupations, also for religious equality and free education. div.head: STANLEY IN ENOLAND.
div.p: STANLEY IN ENOLAND.

Mr. H. M. Stanley arrived at Dover by the Ostend boat at a quarter to four on Saturday afternoon, and met with an enthusiastic reception, The Mayor of Dover, preceded by his mace-bearer, and accompanied by the Town-clerk and Councillors of Dover, boarded the steamer, and an address of vvelcome was read. Mr. Stanley was warmly cheered from the shore. Owing to faulty police arrangements the depbta- tion from the Emin Relief Committee had such great difficulty in getting through the crowd that Mr. Stanley, in proceeding to the railway carriage, was so closely hemmed in that he could not lift his hat to acknowledge the cheers. Accompanying the great ex- plorer were Captain Nelson, Dr. Parke, Mr. Jephson, Lieutenant Stairs, Mr. Wilson, and Sir Wm. Mackinnon. On arrival in London, where he was vociferously cheered by large crowds, Mr. Stanley entered the Bareness Bur- dett Coutte carriage and drove to the house taken for him at Der Vera Gardens, Kensington. By desire of the Prince of Wales, Mr. Stanley on Saturday evening left London for Sandringham, where he will remain on a visit till Monday. There is a rumour that Mr. Stanley will shortly pro- ceed to the Congo as Governor-General, with absolute power from the King, by whom he is still retained, to do what he thinks best to place the Free State on a solid administrative basis, and to take whatever steps he deems necessary for the development of its resources.

With the aid of the wind and the sun at their backs, Warrington at the onset compelled their opponents to adopt the defensive: Borthwick's. kick off gravitated into touch near the half way flag,. and although Halton ta-.lcled Boscow with the oval in his possession, Berry, 'rhorniley, and Littlewood dribbled excellently to half way, where Bate secured from a pack, and feigning to pass as he travelled he tricked hi a oppo- nents until within a few yards from the line, and being finally tackled he passed to Fair Turner, who, when pressed, handed over the charge to Ashton, and a pretty piece of play resulted in a try, J. Halton had an,opening,, but the tackling was safe, and Lawless who had not displayed anything like his proper form, happily made no mistake this time, and brought his man to grass. Sudlow put in an excellent run along the popular side, and from some scrambling and faulty play by Warrington, McLelly scored, Graham failing at the place. This was St. Helens' last chance, for the Warringtonians now warmed to their work, and at once made matters lively for their opponents. A fiae forward movement headed by Fair Turner and Povey, took play to the visiting quar- ter flag, when a fine passing movement among the , home backs saw Evans racing, over the line, but unfortunately for him he had stepped into touch. This ill-luck seemed to rouse the homesters to further exertions, for on the restart T. He, as it were, mesmerized his oppon- ents with his tricky antics, and running through the thick of his opponents, baffied all their efforts to stay his progress, and a brilliant piece of play resulted in a try, which J. ST. HELENS OLD BOYS V. WYCLIFFE.—The St. Helens Old Boys first team played their concluding fixture on Saturday, when they defeated the Wycliffe team by a try and four minors to two minors. ST. HELENS OLD BOYS V. HALTON VlEW.—These teams met at Farnworth on Thursday week, a pleasantly con- tested and enjoyable game ending in a victory for the Boys by two goals and three minors to one goal,two tries, and four minors.

WARRINGTON "A " v. RUNCORN " A."—Although Warrington succeeded in inflicting a decided reverse on the premier " A " team of Cheshire, the interest in the return match had not abated one iota, for fully 4,000 people assembled at Wilderspool enclosure on Monday evening to witness the return engagement. The contest was favoured with beautiful weather, and as the proceeds were devoted to the widows and orphans occasioned by the recent Llanerch Colliery disaster, a good sum should be handed over to this deserving charity. Both sides were thoroughly representative, and Runcorn winning the toss started towards the pavilion goal, play settling at midfield. Rowe passed smartly to Mather, who got grandly away, but his final pass was forward, and scrimmages monopolized the game for a time. Runcorn ' by a combined dribble relieved to centre, but a flying kick by Jolley resulted in Webster getting possession, and owing to a slight misunderstanding amongst the Runcornians, he ot a try behind the posts. Following the drop out a kick by Jolley forced a minor. Boscow replied grandly to the drop out, and for a time the visitors were press,-d, but May relieved finely. Jolley then got away but threw forward, and play raged in neutral territory. Some fine passing then ensued between Rowe, Mather, Jolley, and Webster, but the last- named was floored before getting dangerous. Immediately after a grand chance was missed, and then Houghton kicked splendidly to midfield. Ashton, Eyres, and Berry were conspicuous by

retaliated, and being supplemented by a run from Houghton, the quarter flag was reached. Then ensued some pretty passing by Hulse, Hughes, and Hancock, Wit a wild pass spoiled a grand chance. Boscow next relieved in fine style, and the play was again in the visitor's territory. Runcorn by some very fine defensive play repeatedly kept their opponents at bay, although Jolley and Rowe were within an ace of scoring. By the aid of a bad pass the visitors managed to get away to centre, and the position was improved by a kick from the ruck. Some very pretty passing , between Hughes, Houghton, and Stubbs was cheered, and Robinson by a smart run and kick transferred the game to the home lines. Thomiley, however, relieving. A fine bit of passing between Hollingworth, Davies. Houghton, and Cawley would have resulted in a sure try, but for a timely.tackle by Webster. Subsequently Berry, Davies, Eyres, and Tliorniley dribbled to mid- field, but again Runcorn attacked.. Jolley and May were loudly cheered for fine pieces of play. Houghton then kicked to Boscow, who was cheered for a grand piece of play', and half time was called with Warrington 0-2-1 to nil. Resuming, Runcorn started, and the open- items saw the game at the centre flag. A free kick to Runcorn improved their position, but Thorniley getting away, passed te Jolley, who punted neatly over May's head, but Robinson was the saviour of his side with an excellent kick back to the quarter flag. Rowe, Mather, and Holmes passed well, but the advantage was prompt- ly neutralized by Davies. However, froina. scrimmage, fine passing by the home backs raised the- siege on the Runcorn goal, and a screw kick by Jolley was negatived by a sharp burst of passing of the Runcorn forwards. The previous exertions- of the match had efFect on both teams, and the match stowed down somewhat, Runcorn if anythinghaving the advantage. Rowe and Byres drib- ' bled grandly, and the Runcorn goal was again in serious jeopardy. Faulty play by the home backs gave Run- corn an opening, but Roscow was as safe as usual, and Warrington were still on the aggressive. Davies (War- rington) came away with an excellent run and pass to Webster, who ran to the Runcorn twenty-five., Ashton next got away, and only the sure tackling of the-visiting backs prevented disaster.. A smart drop by Webster nearly had the desired effect, and May touched down. Ashton and Mather nearly scored from sterling runs, and Runcorn saved from a free kick taken by Jolley.' .T.ndici- ous kicking by the Runcorn backs changed the venue- to the home quarters. A capital piece of play by Webster Iwas feebly responded to by his comrades. The game was worked dangerously near the visiting goal, until Lee got away with an accurate dribble, transferring the game to the Warrington end. Relief was brought about by Caw- ley, and directly after the whistle sounded "No side," the final score being as follows :---Warrington, ; Runcorn, nil. The game was of a too monotonous des- cription to call for c.omment„and as the play was chiefly ' confined to the forwards and half backs, who had a ' strong tendency to hug the oval, the game was some- what tiring to witness, thongh there were instances, of exceptional brilliancy shown. Teams :—Warrington ; Boscow, back; Webster, jolley, and Heesom, three- quarter backs • Rowe and Mather, half backs; Thorni- ley, Isherwood, Davies, Knowles, Molyneux. Berry,. Holmes, Eyres, and A.shton, forwards.. Runcorn: May, . back; Cawley, Houghton, and Rnbinsen, three-quarter backs; Davies and Hollingworth, half backs; Hulse, I Clarke, Stubbs,lJughes, Williams, Lee, Hancock, Dutton, and Derbyshire, forwards. WEST LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. WARRINGTON V. ST. RULERS.

The final stage of the above-named competition, also the football season proper in Warrington. was brought to a conclusion on Saturday, when our local ,club encountered St. Helens in the return League match. The first match, which was the opening of this season's campaign, resulted in a victory for the Warringtonians by a goal, although the St. Helens team, it must be ad- mitted, caught the Wa,rringtonians at their worst, as was witnessed by the four successive -defeats experienced by them in their next engagements, The hopes of St. Helens reversing the first result were certainly never dreamt of, and the large crowd who assembled on Satur- day came with the expectation of seeing Warrington pile on a scorewhich would almost establish a record In this they were disappointed, for with the absence of eight of their prominent players, the combination was, upset... . . .

St. Helens wereweaklv represented, and arriving late, it was fully an hour after the advertised time when Fair Turner set the oval in motian towards the pavilion goal, free kicks being witnessed along the popular side. After these opening movements the first to show up was Ash- ton and Jolley, win made a welcome re-appearance, and in conjunction with Berry dribbled the oval to near the Saints' line, where Rowe dribbled from the pack, and Sudlow was compelled to save. The drop-out found the. oval at half-way, and a kick by Evans, supplemented by a run by Ashton, severely harrassed the visiting defence. T. Jolley next got awa% , but the tackling was safe, and . .

The following is the record for the season that is iistt passed, of some.well-known Lancashire clubs. Swinton' have won 24 games, have di.awn five, and have been, vanquished fivetimes. Twenty-three victories stand to the credit of Satlinrd, while on, the other side there are' nine defeats, sii,s ganses having been di-avro. Wigan has been about the most successfalof Lancashire clubs. It has passed through the Lancashire League contest with- out being beaten; . scoring 11. goals' and 25 tries, as against four goals and one try. lh its club games it has compiled 34 goals and 61 tries, as 'l4' goads and 16 tries. • The Broughton team has not done well,, as there stand against it 14 defeats as against nine. wins and eight draws. Broughton Rangers woir 14; lost 154, and drew three games. Manchester Rangers' record stands thus,: 16 victories, 10 defeats, 7 draws. The Free Wanderers have had so bad A time of it, that they should really consider the proprietrof becoming defunct.

Of the counties Yorleihire were easily first,se they not only went through their nine fixtures-unbeaten, but had the gratification r,f asserting their title to the champion- ship by taking down the. rest of England. Lancashire may .be said to have done fairly well. They were decidedly unfortunate taliose their match with- York- shire, as the try which gave the day to the latter was of a. doubtful nature. The-reverse by Westmorland came as a suiprise, Lancashire underrating their opponents in addition to being poorly represented.. Cheshire can only point to one win out'ef five fixtures—not a flatter- tog record by any means. Of the northern comities, there was little difference between Durham and Gimbel.- ' land, both coming out better than Northumberland and Westmorland. Middlesex was by far ' the best of the southerners, as they beat both Kent and Surrey. and r gave Yorkshire a good game:

Neither Warrington nor St. Helens put wstrong team in the field on Saturday, bub the Warringtonians- had decidedly the upper hand bcth in the ' score-and the play. St. Helens showed a weakness and a want of combination which easily account for the very indiffer- ent season they have had. In no part did they show any brilliancy or finish. Their forward play was not vigorous, while behind then, was scarcely' an attempt at anything like judicious passing. The result was a fair indication of the respeCtive merits of the two teams.

The meeting of Warringtediarid St. Helens Recs. Is air interesting event at any time, but, to-day it will be- doubly interesting. In this district there are three clubsl which may very fairly claim precedence over others, ancli none of which will admit they are in any way inferior to the others. These are Warrington, St. Helens Recs. and Runcorn. The Recs. and Runcorn had a meeting on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and the hon- ours of the day were so equally balanced that the game bad tube drawn. To-day the Recs. met Warrington on the Wilderspool ground in aid of the • local gymnasium, and it is yet to be decided whether the wirepullers will fare better or worse than the "wearers of the green." The last time the two clubs encountered each other there was a draw, and it will show a remarkable equal- ity among the three clubs named if the result is the same on this occasion.

The football season is now at ani end; .and amongst the records of local clubs there is not one of a more disastrous character than that of Widnes. Oat of 39' matches played ,no less than 20 have been lost and 5 drawn. 'While only a third, i.e. 14, have been won. The total score reads: Widnes 23 goals, 44 tries, and 75 minors to opponent 24 goals, 39 tries, and 68 minors. Nearly every match played away from home was lost, ,and had it not been fora remarkable revivifying of the old bones during Easter week, when four successive victorieswere secured, the results of the season would havebeeo still more un- pleasant reading. There is plenty of material in Widnes for forming a first class team, but at the present time there is a lamentable lack of esprit devorps °amongst the members and a marked lack of combihation on the field. Until an alteration takes place in these matters defeat and disaster may be expected.

Runcorn brought their season to a., close on Saturday, when they had a visit from St Helens Recreation, and about five thousand spectators gathered to witness the encounter, about 1,500 travelling from .3t. Helens. The game was remarkably well-contested throughout,, and there was more tackling than has been seen on the Run- corn field for many a long day. On four occasionshad the game to he stopped through a St. Helens man being placed hors de combat from some cause or other' and Roble, who sustained an injury to his leg had to retire early in the second half.

The most conspicuous man on the field was Tommy Davies, who ran, dodged, and kicked in a manner that caused huge delight to those present. He had many a narrow escape from scoring. Despite betng a "marked man," and severely watched, Crompton ' succeeded it crossing the St. Helens line and kicked a goal from the place. A tremendous cheer was raised'when he registered the try which was his sixtieth during the season, a record that will not be beaten by any centre three- quarter in England.

Houghton at full back played a camtal game and Evans at half back was in grand formiand gave•the men behind him plenty to do. The point wlnch equalised the game was a piece of good luck,. and was scored in tho. second half. Seddon made a capital return •to a kick by Davies and the St. Helens forwards waiting offside rushed at Crompton who fumbled the ball, which whs rushed over the line and Matthews dropped upon it. The kick by the same player, which added the premier point, was a splendid one. The score was Runcorn 1 . goal 3 minors, St. Helens Recreation I.goal 2 minors.

For the coming season-the—li—u—ni:Orn Cricket Club will not have a very busy season, as only.half,a.dozen matchea have been arranged. A lawn tennis court has been marked out on the field, and the introduction of this game is the reason for the decline of the cricket fixtures, which must be a matter of regret to the followers of the manly sport. Lawn tennis is not an exciting pastime, and incomparison with cricket,, it is, speaking colloqu- ially, "simply nowhere," and it is a pity that the Cricket Club have made cricket take a back, seat by in- troducing tennis.

Warrington opened their list of fixtures.on Saturday, with an even game against St. Helens, though the re- praTntatives pi the glass slaking town came out with an advantage of five runs. The match, so far as War- rington was concerned, was chiefly notable for the, goucl bowling of J. J. Crosfield, and the promising batting of Wagstaff, the new professional.

Early on Sunday afternoonrthe body of a work- man was found in the Ship Canal cutting near Hollins Green with a bullet wound in the right side. The deceased man was named Thomas Ellainan, ind was a native of Gloucestershire, but had workee on the canal 'since the beginning of the undertaking. Tor three or four months back he had lodged with Joseph Arstall, a shoemaker, who lives at Rixton- 'lane ends, about a quarter of a mile to the west of HollinstOreen. Ellaman was an engine tenter, and about nine o'clock on Sunday night he left his lodgings to go to the canal to take charge of Wiat was known as the "Rocker" pnmp on the Warlon- ton side of the cutting. About two o'clock in the afternoon, Arstall took Ellaman's dinner down to the canal, but not finding his lodger in the pumping station he looked around and at length found hitrylymg on his back at the bottcnrof the canal. Arstall at fret thought Ellaraan was in a fit, but failing to restore animation, he looked mind and saw on the on- '-oankmnt at the other side of the canal the engine tender of the " boiler " pump there and who is spoken of by the names of Vane-lan and Bent. He shouted to him to• F. and seek the walking ganger from the huts. This Vaighan did, and the walk- ing ganger, Westail,• was soon on the spot, Vaughan following a few minutes later: More efforts were made' to resuscitate Ellaman, but as all these-were unavailing • the conclusion was come to that he waw dead, and the local policeman, P.C. Schofield,. was sent for. The body was then removed tooArstall's house. Tip to this time, what was afterwarth found to be the real • cause of death was never Suspected, as no blood was visible about the deceased man's Clothesi and it was not till his vestments were removed at arstalifs house that the bullet wound was noticed in the right side.' Oh this discovery being made P.C. Schofield was again, of course, at once commu- nicated with.

On further inquiries being mad it was- soon found that the man Yaughan had disappeared. After seeking Westall and coming back to where Miamian lay, he had, acting under the instructions of Westall, gone to look at the deceased man's pump • which he reported to be all right, but after the others had let with the body he is said to have been seen crossing the fields to. the Man- chester-road, on gaining which he strtlck off through Hollins Green in the direction of Manchester.. Since then his whereabouts has not been discovered,, although an active search has been instituted by-the There are several circumstances whichthrow a partial light ors the mysterious affair. It seems that both Ella. man and Vaughan were possessed of revolvers. Ella,mart had only-bought his pistol on the Saturday night at War- rington,together with a nuMber of cartridgesr and on Saturday night he showed the-weapon to-his landlord, explaining as he did so that he had bought it as be intended shortly to sail for Australia where he had some relatives. After the cause of death had been ascertained a search was made for the revolver, without 9tifte.9ls lot sane time, but at length it was found, togetherwiththe cart- ridges, at the bottom of the deceased's melodian box. It was then seen that the bullet which had caused the death - was a smaller one than would be -fired from, Ellaman's own revolver, which indeed showed no -signonf having been fired Mall. This, of course, apparently disposed of any theory of suicide. It seems that Viughamhad had his revolverin his possession for several- months,. and it is said, that so lately as Saturday nightihehad,been dis- playing it Ora raslo and reckless fashion-gn a beerhouse at Hollins Green, and offering to make wood any dam- age if one of the parties would let him put a bullet through his hat: These circumstanceerhave led tb a con- jecture that on Sunday morning Vaughan was still in the humour for playing with his dangerous tnyrwith a result in this ease of the most unfortunate description. ft does not seem that there was any 111-wilt between Ellaman and Vaughan. The former;.indeed,,was not -known-to have any enemies, as he was -a* harmless and, inoffensive man. _ _ _

A SHIP CANAL BETWEEN THE MID- LANDS AND THE MERSEY. The "Birmingham Daily Post" says during the summer Of 1888 a largely attended public meeting was field at the Queen's Hotel, Birmingham, to consider a scheme suggested by Mr. Beriah H. Shepherd, engineer, for the construction of a canal to place Birmingham and the Midlands in direct communication with the sea vg, the Weaver Navigation and the River Mersey. A few months later a Sub-Committee, which had been appointed to examine the project, reported generally in its favour, and it was resolved to open a guarantee fund, and to undertake a complete detailed survey of the whole route. Little has been heard of the matter lately, but we un- derstand that it has been pushed forward diligently, and, having regard to the magnitude of the undertaking, considerable progress has been made. In the firstviace, the detailed survey has been made, this work having Ilen entrusted to Sir James Brunlees and Mr. M'Kerrow, of Westminster, in co-operation as regards certain features of the scheme with Mr. Edwin Clark, the elainent hydraulic engineer. At their suggestion and that of some of the principal landowners upon the route, nue modifications of the course of the proposed canal "ave been adopted, which it is believed will be a. con- siderable improvement. Various negotiations have also ha been carried on whereby the obtaining of Par- -I'e authority , for the project will be faci- - tate& The application to Parliament is now the Itext important step to be taken, and at their rast meeting, which was held on Thursday, the :'elnmittee approved of stops being taken with this oh- lect• The project, we are informed, has been very fav- ourably received by the various landowners along the touts, and receives support from the Weaver Navigation A.!ust, the Manchester Ship Canal, and the authorities ,?Itl the Mersey Docks. It is estimated, therefore, that co £3O e st of obtainingan Act of Parliament will notexceed I• ,000. Notices will be given km a Bill to be introduced nto Parliament next session. Since the project was first 'Fought forward an important alteration has been srided upon. It was originally proposed that the canal I.„Yuld be 14ft in depth, with a minimum width of 601 t., ;;;It under the advice of Sir .T. Brunless and Mr. llerrow, the width will be increased to 72ft. This will rignu a cataal of sufficient capacity to accommodate sea, ng vessels of 300 tons burthen, or barges of 400 tons. ,n.otable feature in the scheme is the large extent to :In locks, as a means of ascending from a low level to or vice versa, will be replaced by a Z system. of uraulic lifts such as are now in use on several contla Lel canals. The total cost of the canal is estimated at 11;°113 two and a half to three millions sterling. The pro- ertoters of the scheme assure us that they have been much b„eauraged by the manner in which it has been received tfl'epersons of great influence, and if they can obtain cap'itt act of Parliament they have confidence that the tottialg forconstructing the canal will be readily forth- n.

div.head: TRAGEDY AT ERITH.
div.p: THE TRAGEDY AT ERITH.

The inquest on the bodies of William A. Cook, 35, and Elizabeth Sarah Cook, 34, who were found dead in bed, with their throats cut, at Garden Cottage, Stades Green, Erith, on Saturday, was opened on Tuesday, at the vill- age schoolroom, by Mr. Carttar, coroner. The bodies lay side by side on a bed in the house where the tragedy took place. Evidencewas given that the deceased man had been worried about his work. For twenty-three ye ars he had been employed on the South-Eastern Railway, but he threw it up, as he said his superiors found fault with him, and he could do nothing to please them. He had complained of pains in the head, but it was not sun- posed he was insane.—The jury found that Cook murdered his wife, and afterwards committed suicide, and that at the time he was of unsound mind.

The enjoyment of sound health of body, next to -ttno of sound health of mind, is one of the gtsatest -of terrestrial bles-ings. and a few plain observations ou the -vest mode of obtaining this state of physical -miniort may be perused with advantage. T'ue science of preserving health is gnuerally c,ompre- bended miller the term Di*teriem, which ilea a rso et. -ence to cleanliness, the prep.,' »thin arm CO.flbLitoptlon of food, air, ereicise, reat;the passions...sleep, and -other matters connected with the function of the body. Atoongtheloweraniruals, who are governed by an linen lug inst Met, there is no ma a foram correction of abuses hi the healthful preservation of the tioay; put man, who is the creature of circumstances. and who has been left to be governed by his reason so as to 7 snit his taste and convenience, stands constantly in need of advice on the general head :4 just referred to- Our artificial mode of living, the prodigious variety of our-employments in and out of doors, our different modes of dwelling and dressing, the endless variety •of substances used as food and drink, the great • diversity of national customs and manners, the difference and changeableness of climate, and our vicious indulgences, have all a powerful influence on our physical welfare. By our present mode of -living we are certainly stronger in frame and of . greater longevity than savages (though there is a prejudice to the contrary), but we pay the penalty of this superiority in our liability -to numberless complaints originating in the artificial habits of &valet life.

I do not imagine that persons who live in ordinary intercourse with society can pretend to exist like . anchorites, or follow every rule laid down for the -preservation of their health; but I do believe that, with a little firmness and no great sacrifice of feeling, a very excellent state of health may be obtained, even with our present artificial practices. All who have studied the condition of the human body lay down personal cleanliness as the first thing to be attained in the pursuit of health, and with- out this all other means will prove abortive. The outer skin of the human body is composed of the most minute scales, between which are interstices, or openings, called pores, from whence constantly •exude the liquid matter which we denominate pers- piration, but which is, in fact, the refuse of the internal blood. The quantity of p, rspiration daily -exuded, under ordinary circumstances, is. from one to two pounds weight, and it is essential to our existence that this should be projected outwards. AS the clothes worn next the body act as sponges for the receipt of perspirable matter they should in- variably be preserved in the most cleanly condition, for if they be soiled or impure, they will not receive the liquid effusion, which is consequently lodged on the skin, and returned to the internal parts by the absorbents, greatly to the injury of the health. It is impossible to lay too much stress on this most important fact in dietetics. The clothes, whether of woollen or linen, worn next the skin, should be frequently changed—the oftener the better; but even this precaution, excellent as it is, will not pre- serve uniform sound health, unless the skin be from time to time thoroughly purified with water. The inhabitants of this country, and indeed of most countries, are culpably negligent in not generally attending to this point in cleanliness. Almost all the great law-givers and founders of religion, from the remotest antiquity, seem to have been aware of the influence of personal cleanliness ' upon the moral character of man, and have strongly inculcated it. In many cases it has; been interwoven with the most solemn rites of pub- lic and private worship; and is so still, in a particu- lar manner, in Mahommedan countries. Let all clothes, linen, beds, blankets, and other articles coming in contact with the body, be kept in the most eleanly condition—that is, free of the perspired matter. Let the body, and particularly the joints, be frequently washed with pure water, especially in summer. The face, neck, and hands, ought to be daily washed, both morning and even- ing. In washing the face, the cold water should be always laved behind the ears and on the back part of the neck, by which practice toothache will in a great measure be prevented. The Month should be well rinsed every morning with water, and the teeth simultaneously rubbed with the finger, which is considered to be better than a brush. It has been found that frequent shaving of the beard is conducive to free perspiration, and, con- sequently, to health. I would particularly recom- mend that the teet be very frequently washed. If bathed every morning in cold water, the complaint of cold feet, now so prevalent, would seldom be lend, Bathing Of every description is the basis of cleanliness, and may be pronounced one of the most beneficial restorers of health and vigour. To per- sons enjoying a perfect state of bodily vigour, the frequent use of the bath is less necessary than to the infirm, as the healthy possess a greater power te resist infirmities by means of their unimpaired per- spiration, the elasticity of their minute vessels, and the due consistence of their circulating fluids. The case is very different with the infirm, the delicate., and the aged. In these the slowness of circulation, the viscidity or clamminess of the fluids, the con- stant efforts of nature to propel the impurities towards the skin, combine to render the frequent bathing or washing of their bodies an essential requisite to their physical existence. Although most persons acknowledge the propriety of frequent bodily ablution there are not many who are fond of putting their belief in practice; they will tell yoa that they have no time, no conveniency, for bath- ing. But these are frivolous excuses. It is their indolence which afflicts them ; and rather than clean themselves, they will run the chance of having their health impaired, and live in a state of per- petual bodily discomfort, Every one has the use ol water, and could easily spare a few minutes for so . highly beneficial a process as washing themselvee. On the other hand, those who indulge in the judi- cious practice of bathing enjoy a more active state of body and more durable state of robust health than those who do not. Bathing may be performed with hot or cold water, according as feelings dic- tate, or circumstances permit. The lukewarm or tepid bath, from 85 to 96 degrees of heat, is always safe; and the temperature may be raised to 101 degrees without danger to healthy persons. So fax is the hot bath from relaxing the tone of the solids, that it may justly be considered as one of the most powerful restoratives with which we are acquainted. Instead of heating the body it has a cooling effect, and diminishes the quickness of the pulse. Hence, tepid baths are of eminent service, where the body has been overherheated, from whatever cause, whether after fatigue from travelling, severe bodily exercise, or after violent exertion and perturbation of mind. By their softening and moistening power, they greatly contribute to the formation and growth of the body of young persons. Bathing in rivers, as well as in the sea, is effec- tual for every purpose of cleaning the body; it washes away impurities from the surface, opens the cutaneous vessels for a due perspiration, and in- creases the circulation of the blood. For these reasons it cannot be too much recommended, not only to the infirm and debilitated, under certain restrictions, but likewise to the healthy. Sea water Is most efficacious as a cold bath, for there is a stimulating quality in the salt which gives a grate- fnl glow to the skin. There is a popular belief that it is necessary to plunge head foremost into the water, else a determination of blood to the head takes place, and headaches, Sac., follow. Nothing can be more erroneoua A sudden plunge is often productive of mischief, but it is not necessary to wet the whole head in bathing, especially if there be too much hair, which afterwards, taking a long time to dry, is often inconvenient. Whenever after a short immersion in the cold bath the individual feels chill, his skin pale, and the lips and nails of a purrtiih hue, it is a proof. that cold bathing does _not agree with Lim.

A WALK ON THE SHIP CANAL.
FROM WARRINGTON TO RUNCORN.

A. TIRED TRAVELLER'S TALE. From Warrington to Runcorn on foot is a serious matter for a man with corns, but when you come to foot it over Ship Canal railway sleepers, and among Ship Canal sand and debris generally, it is really something am ful. An apparent humbug who writes in "The Examiner" occasionally under the name of "Ko-Ro " the other week finished up an article with a sentence about the fields and country lanes, the babbling brooks, and the com- pany of the trilling birds. If the babbling humbug had kept the sentence to himself, it would have been all right, and for anything I 'care he could have listened to the trilling of the birds for many a day to come, but just as it happened he couldn't. hold his peace. Well, the Editor saw that sentence, and it gave him an idea. We suggested that I might go in for a little bit of nature, so to put it, and have a country walk as far as Runcorn. That was very good, but when he broke it gently that I might as well take in the canal at the same time, and so do something to earn my keep, it lather took the gloss off. 'Yes, it's a hard world, and full of pitfalls, and other funny things, but when youv'e got a thing to do you might as well set about and do it. And that's just the case. The Editor wants facts, and if these aren't facts my reputation's gone. However, not to run too far away from the canal, it is really surprising what progress is being made. Starting from Arpley Bridge, it is seen at once that the cutting for the diversion of the river is complete, and nearly full of water, the result of a flood of a few months back. The new bed of the river has been cut acme the fields, and the diverted waterway will regain its old channel just at the near side of Walton Arches. No work is going on at this particular spot at present—the new "cut" is waiting the course of events—and the only sign of canal life is the watchman who, in company with his box, guards the entrance of the path from the trespassing public. At present the grounds of the Warrington Cricket and Bowling Club have not been interfered with. That is to come though, for it is expected that the further corner of the grounds will succumb to the enterprise. The construction of the Warrington docks in this vicinity will, of course, bring about startling changes, and entirely alter the old order of things, but as we have to go to Runcorn, we might as well be proceeding with- out much comment on these developments to come. The most important work going on at present in this neighbourhood is connected with the deviation of the railway lines that run into Bank Quay Sta- tion. in order that they may be raised to a sufficient altitude to cross the canal at a high level. The de- viation of what is known as the Grand Junction Railway, which runs through Moore and Preston Brook to Crewe and the further south, is fairly entered upon. The deviation will begin near the Arches in Slutchees-lane, where we find a number of workmen busily laying foundations. From this point the lane will rise on large embankments at a gradient of one in 135, and will cross the river by a new bridge alongside Walton Arches, and, continu- ing its upward course, will finally reach its highest point on a new viaduct that is to span the Ship Canal, when it will gradually descend until it re- gains its old route. When you arrive at Walton Arches, you see at once that there has been a transformation, though just now work there is going on rather quietly. There are to be two arches on each side of the river, and these are in an advanced state, but some delay is caused by having to wait for the supply ot iron work that is needed. The arch over the river will span 160 feet, and there will be no centre pier. The old canal has, of course, been tilled up. Fur- ther on work is being pushed forward as rapidly as possible in the construction of the viaduct, and it may be mentioned here that Mr. Siduey H. Bow- man Meek, late of the London and North-Western Railway, has charge of these railway deviations, as well as others in this locality.- He is assisted by an able staff, who have their work cut out in superiii- ' tending these gigantic undertakings. At Acton Grange all is bustle. The work s-ops are in full blast, and the clerks in the offices are by no means idle. All round about is stocked an im- mense quantity of material to be brought into use later on, and huge rocks lie here and there in seem- ing, but only seeming, disorder. Engines are puffing, steam cranes are lifting enormous weights, bath of stone and of iron, and there is so much noise and activity that it is a positive treat to take a few more strides Runcorn bound. The continuity of the embankment is broken at Acton Grange, where there is to be a bridge, but as you leave the smoke and din, and get ou towards Moore, you have the embankment again on your right, and the cutting on your left, and there is much to contemplate. Not that there is much going on hereabouts. The cutting is practically completed, and the bottom covered with water, but there is something to think about and notice all the same. The very change that has been wrought in so short a time demands admiration. Nearing Moore, there is additional bridge building going on, in connection with the deviations, but that is about all in the way of actual active operations. The sight of Moore is a grand relief after hunting about for facts, and getting half smothered with sand. In spite of the canal, of the navvies, and everything else, the pretty village looks as pretty as ever. Attired in "new spring costume it is de- lightful, and the contrast from the turmoil of the works to its peace and rusticity is refreshing. There are two stations at Moore, as everyone knows, but there is only one village publichouse, which perhaps everyone doesn't know. It is the dinner hour as I enter the quiet street that boasts of the presence of the Red Lion. As for villagers, there does not ap- pear to be one stirring, but there is a clatter of feet behind, and a little army of canal men pass and are soon gathered in at the Lion. As they walk up the street they look a fine, hgalthy set of men, with plenty of physique, though their language sometimes certainly is rather expressive and free. Of course, I follow them in. In search of information, of course. The workmen, who carry their eatables' with them, take seats in a large room at the back of the house, and in about two seconds there is such a clamour for pints and quarts as you never heard.' " Boys to drink ale " appreciatively observes the landlord, as we sit in the snug after the heat of the battle is over, and the thirsty souls in the back room have ceased to be thirsty. I admit the truth of the observation, and venture a remark on the grist that the works must bring to mine host's mill. Yes, is the reply, he is no doubt receiving a benefit, but it is mainly from visitors to the canal and not so much from the men themselves, as they mostly live in Warrington and Runcorn, being conveyed in a mail night and morning to and from their work. At night, he gives me to understand, the village inn is as quiet as in other and less stirring times, and is even as other village inns. From Moore to Runcorn is a nice walk when you are fit, but when you fall lame—cast a shoe, so to speak—it is a dreary and a weary matter. There is not much to see, and nothing to describe that has not, been described before. A few men are working at this end, but when you pass the Big Field and trudge on to Runcorn everything seems at a stand- still. A solitary group of men are working here and there at intervals, there is only the 4:Yeasional noise of a workshop, and I am told that this part of the canal is going to be left as it is for: a time, while more pressing work is grappled with. About heresl strike a line of sleepers, and stride desper- ately over them for something like a couple of miles Warning boards bear the legend " Beware of the engine." I beware, but as there are no engines about the danger is small. I survive the ordeal, and arrive in Runcorn at last. True, I feel more dead than alive, and have had a " kink "in my leg ever since, but still I live to tell the tale. Say ;do you know what it is to have an appetite, a roaring, raging appetite? No ; you suffer from indigestion. How sad. Well, just walk from Warrington to Runcorn on the Ship Canal, and if you don't acquire an appetite Call me a--. Of course, you mustn't forget the sleepers.

_ A MAN'S MARRIAG'S AND HIS DUTY. A singular case was heard before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. A. Sinclair, at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday. John Smith, of Gladstone-street, FL young man was summoned at the instance of the White Cross Colliery Company, fora breach a the Coal Mines Regulation Act. Mr. J. 0. Swift prose- cuted. It appeared that it was the defendant's duty to examine the working places of the mine before the colliers went down the shaft. The defendant: was married on the 7th April, and failed to carry out his duties on the mornings of the Bth and Orb April. Mr. Swift remarked that the defendant seemed to have the excuse that he was either mar- ried or was about to be married, but when the lives of a number of men were dependent upon his vigilance and upon the examination of the mine, it was felt by the proprietors of the mina that the least the defendant could have done was to have asked permission to stay away or forwarded an intimation to them.—The defendant acknowledged his guilt and was fined 10s. and costa.

ROMAN CATHOLICISM—" MORE FACTS." , Sir,—Your correspondent "A Dissenter" evidently wants to prolong a discussion on the various pointS of the faith and practice of Catholics. I objecteu lin my; letter to the false assertions made by him as regards our belief. It is on this point I want to show your readers that even ii he does not require information whyyls it
that he eannot see plainly, that, we believe a very differ.

ent thing altogether from what he thinks we do- believe. All this argument clearly comes from a misunderstand- ing of the teaching of our holy religion. The fact is that your correspondent stated a " fact " or two, which' are absolutely ne)t facts at all. Let us go back to his first letter and see his statements, which I think have been fully answered in mine of the 19th inst.
To answer all the controversial matter which your corres•

_ pondent draws into his last letter would take more time and attention than I have at present at my disposal. I am. however, prepari%d to argue the points separately, and feel it a duty to bring before your readers " positive facts." Let us calmly investigate whether your corres- pondent was right or wrong in making such statements in the public Press. Ido not care to which denomina, tion your correspondent belongs, but I know that if I were to make groundless accusations against his form of belief that I should be immediately attacked for doing
so. First, your correspondent gently gives the hint that Catholics follow the traditions of men. Surely this is not a fact. No; the fact is that the Catholic rule of

faith is the whole Word of God, understood infallibly in its true sense. Besides the written Word of God in the Bible, there is also the unwritten. Catholics depend certainly on traditional doctrines. They believe that what Christ or His Apostles spoke is as true as what they, wrote, and it is clear that they delivered many truths by wort of mouth which are not written in the Scripture. The truths are considered authentic and divine by Catholics, when it is found that they have been believed by all Christian nsti--,ns, and in every age of the Church. The Scripture authorizes this dependence on traditional doctrine in 2 Thess. li. 15, 2 Cor. iii. 3, 2 These. iii. 8, Rom. vi. 17, 1 Cor. xi. 2, Tim. vi. 20, and numerous other texts to the same effect. God could never have intended the Bible to be our only rule of faith as we have seen that this was impossible. During the first foul hundred years, a few copies written with the pen existed, and they were translated into only one lan- guage yet during this period, whilst the Bible as a rule of faith was a physical impossibility, the whole world was converted. Secondly, your correspondent gives you to understand that Catholics worship the Blessed Virgin Mary as God. Now, allow me to inform him that Catholics do not give her divine honours which belong to God alone. All the honour given to the Blessed Virgin by men does not equal the least one of those countless acts of honour given to her by her Divine Son our Lord, during the time that he lived with her, and St. Joseph at Nazareth, when as we learn from the Gospel He was subject to them. This honour far from distracting from the divine worship due to God is felt by Catholics to be really tokens of respect to our Blessed Saviour, on whose ac- count chiefly we honour her •, in fact we honour her whom he himself has so wonderfully honoured To dis- honour her would be to dishonour Christ. The Blessed Virgin is rightfully called Mother of God. for Jesus Christ God incarnate (that is, God made man), is truly her son as St. Luke (i. 35 expressly states,—"the holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." St. Elizabeth calls the Blessed Twin the "Mother of my Lord" (St. Luke L 43). and the Biassed Virgin called our Saviour" Son" (St. Luke ii. 48.) Any one, therefore, who refuses to her this title of "Mother of God," shows that he does not realize the incarnation of the son of God, and it is needless to add further testi- mony. Even Dr. Pearson a Protestant (Exp. of Creed, p. 178) says :—" We cannot bear too reverend a regard to the" Mother of our Lord "so long, as we give her not that worship which is due unto the Lord himself." Thirdly, I deny that Catholics worship saints, crucifixes and images. This would be idolatry. We must be judged by our intentions ; for we honour Goa. his saints, and men, by the same external acts of kneeling, bowing ' or uncovering of the bead. Rightly to understand the Catholic doctrine, he must bear in mind that the word " worship " has different significations according as it is applied to God, or creatures. Lastly as to the latter part of his letter which is going 11 beyond the ;proper range of argument as far as this point is concerned I shall leave over for a future day for dis- cussion. All I have written here I believe to be trust-- , worthy, and my chief desire is to show your correspond- ' entthat before making such absurd statements he must examine the other side of the question to find out the true facts. Macaulay says—" There is not, and there never was on this earth a work of human policy so well deserving of examination as the Catholic Church." In conclusion, Mr. Editor, Ilseg you to accept this short exposition of what Catho ics really believe on these points, written without prejudice by one who feels it his greatest blessing to be a member of the \ Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, and who cannot help most earnestly wishing that all possessed the same peace of mind which he enjoys in her communion.' Apologizing for trespassing so much on your valuable space,—l remain, yours truly, THOMAS WILLIAMSON.

RUNCORN WESLEYAN METHODIST SOCIETY. Sir,—ln answer to your correspondent (Mr. Taylor). the Wesleyan Methodist Society may give the fullest details as to the receipt and disposal of its funds to the favoured " 80," but there is nothing in the "general rules " to lead the members to expect an account, or even a summary, of the business done at the Quarterly Meetings; and whatever there may be in the "author- ized " instructions te leaders, I have never during a membership of 15 years, heard a resume of LI e proceed- ings of our local authority, nor can llfind a member who has: the only answer obtainable being, "like yourself, I am completely in the dark." "Every treasurer, &c., is a layman, elected annually by laymen." BY whom are the laytnen elected ? As far as I cats learn, the leaders are nominated ht he itinerant Ministers, and the local preachers are " passed" by the same authority (in the first instance). These, I suppose. would be finally accepted by the sixty " leaders and locals; " and as they are self-elected, and appoint their own officers, you will admit, Mr. Editor, that " officially" the rank and file of the church are left without " If I may be allowed to offer a hint, I would humbly suggest that the leaders of each adult class have a printed balance sheet, together with a brief description of the businesis &tie supplied thorn, which theycould have read by the " assatant " (mentioned as a note, in the rules), in the classes; also, previous to the "Quarter Day," the leader might allude to any business expected to come up for debate, and ascertain the wishes of his members, say as to the retention or otherwise of the ministers, or any other important affair, now transacte,l exclusively by the 60 laymen. Our honoured friend (Mr. Taylor), who has done yeo- man service for the connection during many years, has for a lonc, permd been in close communication (through The Queen held a Privy Council meeting at Windsor his family and business relations) with the sayings and Castle-on Thursday afternoon.

In Vienna and other Austrian and Elungarian citiea the demonstration was of . small dirsensions,, and perfect order was pziaserved. In 'Berlin a small pr portion of' workmen took aheliday, and r nowhere throughout the German Empire does the public 'peace appear to have bce.n seriously distashfld. In Paris considerable crowds assembled, but nothing serious occurred ; and the KUM applies to the troatings and pro- cessions which took place in Madrid, Lielon, and Oporto. In Rome the proceionists were orderly: A Hamburg correspondent telegrapbAthat about 18,000 men struck work on Thursday, but they mostly devoted themselves to pionicing in the envilons. A few arrests: were made, but order was generally observed. A Philadelphia correspondent telegraphs that the Chicago meat packing houses have refused the demand for eight hours a day with increased pay. Easy Counting Competition (No. 7). £lO to be given away in cash prizes as follows £5, £2 10s., £1 10s. £1 to those counting most correctly the ]etter "T' in the last three chapters of St. Luke (ordinary Bibles). verses only. If several competitors are correct the £lO will be equally divided. Close May 14th. Entrance fee is. also three halfpenny stamps for printed result on May 16th.—H. JOHNSON, 19, Church-st , Gainsborough.

-.WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS FOR ALL.—The " Midland Prizeries " Second Biblical Competition. Easy Letter Counting Competition. Open to All, £3O will be given away in Cash Prizes I First prize, £lO ; Second I prize, £5; Third prize. £3 ; Fourth prize, £2 , and £lO in prizes of £1 each. A Cash Prize of £1 will be given to each of the first two Lady competitors, and also to the first two Gentlemen competitors sending in correct lists. To those correctly counting the number of " N's " contained in the Book of Judges. Count all letter " N's" (thus "N.n ") both capital and small together, in verses only, right through each chanter. Count no headings or references. Use the ordinary Bible—not the revised version. If more than one sends cor- rect list, prizes will be equally divided between the successful competitors. In competing, write your full name and address plainly, then the number of " found in each of the twenty-one chapters, and total of all. Send list with entrance fee. Postal order 2s. or 26 stamps. Write at foot of list:—" This is entirely my own work. I have not com- pared wit h, seen, nor heard of another person's figures." Work must be kept secret, as we reserve the right to ref we and return any lists which have noebeen fairly worked. Compe- tition closes certain Saturday, 10th May. Prizes all sent certain Tuesday, 20th May, ready for the Whitsuntide it oh' days. Result sheet posted to each competitor same day. Rules are quite easy, but any inquiries may be made.— Address all letters to JOHN ALCOCK, "The Midland Prizeries," Cheadle, Staffs.

FUNERAL OF MR H. COSSHAM, M.P. The funeral of Mr. Handel Cossham at Avonview Cemetery, near Bristol, on Monday afternoon, attracted some 40,000 people. Great crowds assembled along the route. The hearse and mourners left Weston Park, Bath, shortly after one p.m., and reached the cemetery about three o'clock. Owing to the unexpectedly great crowd, the police arrangements proved inadequate, and when the rush came after the mourners had passed numerous deputations were shut out from the grave- side.
